Katalin Berlow Address: (KB, FW) Department of Mathematics, University of California, Berkeley, CA, USA Email address: katalin@berkeley.edu , Anton Bernshteyn Address: (AB) Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles, CA, USA Email address: bernshteyn@math.ucla.edu , Clark Lyons Address: (CL) Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics, Budapest, Hungary Email address: lyons.clark@renyi.hu and Felix Weilacher Email address: weilacher@berkeley.edu
Abstract.

We study the complexity of locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} from the point of view of descriptive set theory, computability theory, and factors of i.i.d. Our results separate various complexity classes that were not previously known to be distinct and serve as counterexamples to a number of natural conjectures in the field.

1.  Introduction

1.1.  Descriptive complexity of LCL problems

A common theme throughout mathematics and computer science is the desire to understand, in rigorous terms, the complexity inherent in various problems of interest. Depending on the subject area, different notions of complexity can be proposed, resulting in different complexity hierarchies. In this paper we investigate the complexity of so-called locally checkable labeling problems on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} from the perspective of descriptive set theory, probability theory, and computability theory. Our contributions separate certain complexity classes that were not previously known to be distinct and serve as counterexamples to an array of natural conjectures. Further results along these lines will be presented in the forthcoming paper [Ber+].

To start, let us identify the class of problems we will be concerned with. In the definition given below, the underlying structure is provided by a group Γ\Gamma (typically assumed to be finitely generated); in our main results, we will have Γ=ℤn\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{n} for n⩾2n\geqslant 2. This definition can also be phrased, somewhat more generally, in graph-theoretic terms, but we will focus on groups for convenience. Extensions of our results beyond the group-theoretic framework are discussed in §6.1.

Definition 1.1 (LCL problems on a group).

A locally checkable labeling (LCL for short) problem on a group Γ\Gamma is a triple Π=(W,Λ,𝒜)\Pi=(W,\Lambda,\mathcal{A}), where:

  • —

    W⊆ΓW\subseteq\Gamma is a finite set, called a window,

  • —

    Λ\Lambda is a finite set whose elements are called labels, and

  • —

    𝒜⊆ΛW\mathcal{A}\subseteq\Lambda^{W} is a family of mappings W→ΛW\to\Lambda, called allowed configurations.

A solution to Π\Pi, or a Π\Pi-labeling of Γ\Gamma, is a function f:Γ→Λf\colon\Gamma\to\Lambda such that for all γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma, the mapping

W→Λ:w↦f⁡(w​γ)W\to\Lambda\ \colon\ w\mapsto f(w\gamma)

is in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The set of all Π\Pi-labelings of Γ\Gamma is called a subshift of finite type (an SFT for short).

The term “locally checkable labeling problem” was introduced by Naor and Stockmeyer [NS95] in a computer science context. At the same time, subshifts of finite type are studied in topological and symbolic dynamics, where they form an important class of dynamical systems [LM95, CC10].

Example 1.2 (Proper kk-colorings of Cayley graphs).

Let Γ=⟨S⟩\Gamma=\langle S\rangle be a group generated by a finite set SS with 𝟏∉S\bm{1}\notin S. The Cayley graph 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(Γ,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\Gamma,S) has vertex set Γ\Gamma and edge set

E(𝖢𝖺𝗒(Γ,S))≔{{γ,σγ}:γ∈Γ,σ∈S}.E(\mathsf{Cay}(\Gamma,S))\,\coloneqq\,\{\{\gamma,\sigma\gamma\}\,:\,\gamma\in\Gamma,\,\sigma\in S\}.

Following a standard set-theoretic convention, we identify each natural number k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} with the kk-element set {0,1,…,k−1}\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}. Given k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, a proper kk-coloring of 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(Γ,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\Gamma,S) is a function f:Γ→kf\colon\Gamma\to k such that f⁡(γ)≠f⁡(δ)f(\gamma)\neq f(\delta) whenever γ\gamma and δ\delta are adjacent in 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(Γ,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\Gamma,S). Note that ff is a proper kk-coloring of 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(Γ,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\Gamma,S) if and only if ff is a solution to the LCL problem Π=(W,Λ,𝒜)\Pi=(W,\Lambda,\mathcal{A}), where

W≔{𝟏}∪S,Λ≔k,and𝒜≔{φ∈ΛW:φ(𝟏)≠φ(σ) for all σ∈S}.W\,\coloneqq\,\{\bm{1}\}\cup S,\qquad\Lambda\,\coloneqq\,k,\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{A}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\varphi\in\Lambda^{W}\,:\,\varphi(\bm{1})\neq\varphi(\sigma)\text{ for all }\sigma\in S\big\}.

In particular, the set of all proper kk-colorings of 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(Γ,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\Gamma,S) is an SFT.

How difficult is it to solve a given LCL problem Π\Pi? This question can be interpreted in a number of ways. For instance, it can be studied from the standpoint of algorithmic decidability; that is, one may seek an algorithm that, given an LCL problem Π\Pi, determines whether Π\Pi has a solution. Such an algorithm exists for LCL problems on ℤ\mathbb{Z} and, more generally, on finitely generated free groups [ABJ18, Prop. 9.3.35]. On the other hand, refuting a conjecture of Wang [Wan61], Berger showed that there is no such algorithm for LCL problems on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} [Ber66]; see also [Rob71] for a simplified proof due to Robinson. Considering other finitely generated groups gives rise to a rich theory and an active research area; see the survey [ABJ18] by Aubrun, Barbieri, and Jeandel for further references.

Another approach to the complexity of LCL problems is provided by distributed computing, the area of computer science concerned with decentralized computational networks. For an introduction to this field, see the book [BE13] by Barenboim and Elkin. Roughly speaking, a distributed algorithm for an LCL problem Π\Pi is a communication protocol that allows autonomous processes placed at the nodes of an underlying graph GG to compute their corresponding labels forming a solution to Π\Pi (in our setting GG is the Cayley graph of Γ\Gamma). Starting with the seminal work of Naor and Stockmeyer [NS95], there has been a concerted effort to obtain a classification of LCL problems according to their distributed complexity. In particular, a series of contributions by a large number of researchers has culminated in a complete characterization of possible complexities of LCL problems on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} [NS95, CKP19, CP19, Bra+17, GRB22] and the free groups 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} [NS95, Bra+16, CKP19, CP19, Cha+18, Bal+21, Cha20, GRB22] in the so-called 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model of distributed computation.

In this paper we study the complexity theory for LCL problems developed using concepts from descriptive set theory. The idea of employing descriptive set-theoretic notions in a combinatorial context dates back to the pioneering work of Kechris, Solecki, and Todorcevic [KST99]. By now it has grown into a fruitful field—called descriptive combinatorics—with many connections to other areas; see [KM20] for a survey by Kechris and Marks, [Pik21] for an introductory article by Pikhurko, and [Ber22a] for an overview of some recent developments. We also direct the reader to [Kec95, Tse22] for general descriptive set theory background. In descriptive combinatorics, instead of simply solving a given LCL problem Π\Pi on a group Γ\Gamma, we work with an action Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X of Γ\Gamma, and our goal is to solve Π\Pi on every orbit of this action in a “uniform” fashion.

Definition 1.3 (Solutions to LCL problems on group actions).

Let Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be an action of a group Γ\Gamma. For an LCL problem Π=(W,Λ,𝒜)\Pi=(W,\Lambda,\mathcal{A}) on Γ\Gamma, a solution to Π\Pi on XX, or a Π\Pi-labeling of XX, is a function f:X→Λf\colon X\to\Lambda such that for all x∈Xx\in X, the mapping W→Λ:w↦f⁡(w⋅x)W\to\Lambda\colon w\mapsto f(w\cdot x) is in 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Given an action Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, any map f:X→Λf\colon X\to\Lambda gives rise to a family of labelings of Γ\Gamma parameterized by the points of XX. Namely, for each point x∈Xx\in X, we have the corresponding mapping fx:Γ→Λf_{x}\colon\Gamma\to\Lambda defined by fx​(γ)≔f⁡(γ⋅x)f_{x}(\gamma)\coloneqq f(\gamma\cdot x) for all γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma. It is then clear that f:X→Λf\colon X\to\Lambda is a solution to an LCL problem Π\Pi on XX if and only if for all x∈Xx\in X, fx:Γ→Λf_{x}\colon\Gamma\to\Lambda is a solution to Π\Pi on Γ\Gamma.

Recall that a group action Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is free if γ⋅x≠x\gamma\cdot x\neq x for all x∈Xx\in X and γ∈Γ∖{𝟏}\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\{\bm{1}\}. It is not hard to see that if Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free action, then any LCL problem Π=(W,Λ,𝒜)\Pi=(W,\Lambda,\mathcal{A}) with a solution on Γ\Gamma also has a solution on XX. Indeed, given a Π\Pi-labeling f:Γ→Λf\colon\Gamma\to\Lambda of Γ\Gamma, we can obtain a Π\Pi-labeling f∗:X→Λf^{*}\colon X\to\Lambda of XX as follows: Form a set X∗⊆XX^{*}\subseteq X consisting of one point from each Γ\Gamma-orbit and then define f∗​(γ⋅x)≔f⁡(γ)f^{*}(\gamma\cdot x)\coloneqq f(\gamma) for all γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma and x∈X∗x\in X^{*}. Note, however, that this construction invokes the Axiom of Choice to establish the existence of the set X∗X^{*}. In particular, there is no reason to expect the function f∗f^{*} to have any desirable topological or measure-theoretic regularity properties.

Example 1.4 (Proper 22-coloring on ℤ\mathbb{Z}).

Consider the group ℤ\mathbb{Z}. The Cayley graph G≔𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤ,{1})G\coloneqq\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z},\{1\}) is a path which is infinite in both directions. Let Π\Pi be the proper 22-coloring problem for GG (as described in Example 1.2). It is then easy to see that ℤ\mathbb{Z} has a Π\Pi-labeling, namely the map ℤ→2\mathbb{Z}\to 2 sending each k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} to 00 if kk is even and 11 if kk is odd. (The only other Π\Pi-labeling of ℤ\mathbb{Z} sends kk to 00 if kk is odd and 11 if kk is even.) It follows that every free action ℤ⮌X\mathbb{Z}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X admits a Π\Pi-labeling f:X→2f\colon X\to 2. However, such a Π\Pi-labeling ff often must exhibit various pathological properties.

For example, suppose that T:X→XT\colon X\to X is an aperiodic invertible measure-preserving transformation on a standard probability space (X,μ)(X,\mu) such that T2T^{2} is ergodic. (There are many examples of such transformations, for instance the rotation of a circle by the angle α​π\alpha\pi for fixed α∈ℝ∖ℚ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.) Iterating TT gives rise to a free action ℤ⮌(X,μ)\mathbb{Z}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}(X,\mu) defined by k⋅x≔Tk​(x)k\cdot x\coloneqq T^{k}(x) for all k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} and x∈Xx\in X. We claim that, although XX does have a Π\Pi-labeling, no Π\Pi-labeling of XX can be μ\mu-measurable. Indeed, if f:X→2f\colon X\to 2 were a μ\mu-measurable Π\Pi-labeling of XX, then A≔f−1​(0)A\coloneqq f^{-1}(0) and B≔f−1​(1)B\coloneqq f^{-1}(1) would be μ\mu-measurable sets that partition XX and satisfy T⁡(A)=BT(A)=B, hence μ⁡(A)=μ⁡(B)=1/2\mu(A)=\mu(B)=1/2. At the same time, T2​(A)=AT^{2}(A)=A, so by the ergodicity of T2T^{2} we must have μ⁡(A)∈{0,1}\mu(A)\in\{0,1\}, a contradiction.

By adding extra regularity constraints, we arrive at the following definition, which introduces the “big four” complexity classes studied in descriptive combinatorics:

Remarks 1.6.
  1. (i)

    Since the topology on Λ\Lambda is discrete, a labeling f:X→Λf\colon X\to\Lambda is Borel, μ\mu-measurable, Baire-measurable, or continuous if and only if for every label λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, its preimage f−1​(λ)f^{-1}(\lambda) is a Borel, μ\mu-measurable, Baire-measurable, or clopen subset of XX respectively.

  2. (ii)

    In the definition of 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BOREL}(\Gamma), XX can be assumed to be any particular uncountable standard Borel space, for example, the unit interval [0,1][0,1], the real line ℝ\mathbb{R}, or the Cantor space 2ℕ2^{\mathbb{N}}. This results in no loss of generality due to the Borel isomorphism theorem [Kec95, Thm. 15.6].

  3. (iii)

    We stress that in the definition of 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma), the action Γ⮌(X,μ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}(X,\mu) need not be measure-preserving. (However, see Question 6.10.)

  4. (iv)

    Recall that a topological space is zero-dimensional if it has a base consisting of clopen sets. The assumption that XX is zero-dimensional in the definition of 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(Γ)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\Gamma) guarantees that the family of continuous functions X→ΛX\to\Lambda is sufficiently rich to make the definition nontrivial.

The following relations between these classes hold for every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma:

𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(Γ)⊆𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Γ)⊆𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)∩𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ).\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\Gamma)\,\subseteq\,\mathtt{BOREL}(\Gamma)\,\subseteq\,\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma)\cap\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma).

The inclusion 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Γ)⊆𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)∩𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BOREL}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma)\cap\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma) is immediate since every Borel function on a standard probability space (resp. on a Polish space) is measurable (resp. Baire-measurable). The inclusion 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(Γ)⊆𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Γ)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{BOREL}(\Gamma) follows from standard results in descriptive set theory [Kec95, §13], which imply that if Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a Borel action on a standard Borel space XX, then there exists a compatible zero-dimensional Polish topology τ\tau on XX making the action continuous.

More is known for specific groups Γ\Gamma. For example, when Γ=ℤ\Gamma=\mathbb{Z} the four classes coincide:

𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(ℤ)=𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤ)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤ)=𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤ).\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{Z})\,=\,\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z})\,=\,\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z})\,=\,\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}).

See [GR21] by Grebík and Rozhoň for a thorough study of this case. On the other hand, for a free group 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} of rank n⩾2n\geqslant 2, the four classes are distinct and linearly ordered by inclusion:

𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(𝔽n)⊊𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(𝔽n)⊊𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)⊊𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n).\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\,\subsetneq\,\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\,\subsetneq\,\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\,\subsetneq\,\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}).

This chain of strict inclusions is established in [Bra+22] by Brandt, Chang, Grebík, Grunau, Rozhoň, and Vidnyánszky,11 1 Technically, the results in [Bra+22] are stated for LCL problems on unlabeled regular trees, but virtually the same arguments apply in the setting of 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}-actions. building on and synthesizing numerous earlier results in descriptive combinatorics, distributed computing, ergodic theory, and probability theory [Ber23, Ber23a, Mar16, CP19, BGH19, CK13, CMT16, CM16]. For sufficiently large nn, the three classes 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{F}_{n}), 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}), and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) are distinguished by the proper kk-coloring problem (see Example 1.2), since the smallest kk such that the proper kk-coloring problem for the standard Cayley graph of 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} belongs to a given complexity class is 2​n+12n+1 for the class 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) [KST99, Mar16], (2+o⁡(1))​n/log⁡n(2+o(1))n/\log n for the class 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) [Ber22, Ber23, RV17], and 33 for the class 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) [CM16].

In this paper we are interested in another natural class of groups, namely ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} for n⩾2n\geqslant 2. In contrast to the ℤ\mathbb{Z} case, for n⩾2n\geqslant 2 we have the following strict inclusion:

𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(ℤn)⊊𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn),\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\,\subsetneq\,\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}),

because the proper 33-coloring problem for the standard Cayley graph of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} belongs to the class 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) but not 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), as shown by Gao, Jackson, Krohne, and Seward [Gao+24, Gao+18]. In general, the class 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is relatively well understood, thanks to the work of Gao and Jackson [GJ15], Gao, Jackson, Krohne, and Seward [Gao+18], Grebík and Rozhoň [GR23], and the second named author [Ber23a]. For example, it is known that 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is precisely the class of LCL problems on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} solvable by a sublogarithmic-time algorithm in the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model of distributed computation. This is a general result that holds for arbitrary countable groups [Ber23a, Thm. 1.15]; for a detailed discussion of the ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} case, see [GR23, §7.1].

Much less is known about the classes 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}). In particular, it has been a major open problem whether any of them are distinct (see, e.g., [GR21, GR23]):

Question 1.7.

For n⩾2n\geqslant 2, are any of 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) distinct?

Here we partially answer Question 1.7 by exhibiting an LCL problem on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} for each n⩾2n\geqslant 2 that belongs to 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) but not 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}):

It remains an open problem to determine whether 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)=𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})=\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}).

In addition to making progress on Question 1.7, Theorem 1.8 refutes a piece of conventional wisdom in descriptive combinatorics. Although measure and Baire category may behave quite differently [Oxt80], in practice it is usually easier to solve an LCL problem Baire-measurably rather than μ\mu-measurably, and a natural expectation is that 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)⊆𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma) for every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma. While this is true when Γ\Gamma is a free group, and no counterexamples have been known before, Theorem 1.8 shows that this inclusion fails for Γ=ℤn\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{n} with n⩾2n\geqslant 2.

1.2.  Shift actions: the universal domain for descriptive combinatorics?

While the complexity classes described in Definition 1.5 contain LCL problems that can be solved on all free actions of Γ\Gamma with specified regularity properties, it also makes sense to restrict one’s attention to particular actions of special interest. One such action is the shift:

Definition 1.9 (Shift action).

Let Γ\Gamma be a group and let XX be a set. We use 𝒮⁡(X,Γ)≔XΓ\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma)\coloneqq X^{\Gamma} to denote the set of all functions x:Γ→Xx\colon\Gamma\to X. The shift action Γ⮌𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) is given by the formula

(γ⋅x)​(δ)≔x⁡(δ​γ)for all γ, δ∈Γ and x∈𝒮⁡(X,Γ).(\gamma\cdot x)(\delta)\,\coloneqq\,x(\delta\gamma)\quad\text{for all $\gamma$, $\delta\in\Gamma$ and $x\in\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma)$}.

We will only use the above definition for countable (in fact, finitely generated) groups Γ\Gamma. If Γ\Gamma is countable and XX is a standard Borel, (zero-dimensional) Polish, or standard probability space, then so is 𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) equipped with a suitable product structure, and the shift action Γ⮌𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) is Borel (as well as continuous and measure-preserving when these make sense).

In general, the shift action Γ⮌𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) is not free, so it does not directly fit into the context provided by Definition 1.5. To remedy this, we will only work on the free part of the shift action, i.e., the set ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma) of all x∈𝒮⁡(X,Γ)x\in\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) such that γ⋅x≠x\gamma\cdot x\neq x for every γ∈Γ∖{𝟏}\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\{\bm{1}\}. For a countably infinite group Γ\Gamma and a Polish space XX with |X|⩾2|X|\geqslant 2, the set ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma) is comeager in 𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma). Similarly, if Γ\Gamma is countably infinite and (X,μ)(X,\mu) is a standard probability space, then ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma) is conull in 𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) (with respect to the product measure μΓ\mu^{\Gamma}) unless μ\mu is concentrated on a single point. Therefore, in these cases there is no difference from the point of view of Baire category and measure theory whether one considers the whole space 𝒮⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{S}(X,\Gamma) or just ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma).

The following result shows that shift actions are in some sense “universal” for Borel and continuous solutions to LCL problems:

Theorem 1.10 (Seward–Tucker-Drob [ST16], AB/Seward [Ber23a, Thm. 1.12]).

Fix a finitely generated group Γ\Gamma. In the following statements, Π\Pi is an LCL problem on Γ\Gamma.

  1. (i)

    For every standard Borel space XX of cardinality at least 22, we have

    𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Γ)={Π:Π has a Borel solution on ℱ⁡(X,Γ)}.\mathtt{BOREL}(\Gamma)\,=\,\{\Pi\,:\,\text{$\Pi$ has a Borel solution on $\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma)$}\}.
  2. (ii)

    For every zero-dimensional Polish space XX of cardinality at least 22, we have

    𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(Γ)={Π:Π has a continuous solution on ℱ⁡(X,Γ)}.\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\Gamma)\,=\,\{\Pi\,:\,\text{$\Pi$ has a continuous solution on $\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma)$}\}.
Remark 1.11.

In the papers [ST16, Ber23a] the above results are established in the case when XX has exactly 22 points; the generalization to arbitrary XX of cardinality at least 22 follows since any injection 2→X2\to X gives rise to a continuous Γ\Gamma-equivariant map ℱ⁡(2,Γ)→ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma)\to\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma). (Recall that 22 denotes the set {0,1}\{0,1\}, which we endow with the discrete topology.)

A natural question is whether there is a version of Theorem 1.10 for the classes 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma) and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma). For 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma), some partial results are known. By a theorem of Keane and Weiss [Wei00, Thm. 2], for arbitrary Polish spaces XX, YY of cardinality at least 22, the shift actions Γ⮌ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma) and Γ⮌ℱ⁡(Y,Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}(Y,\Gamma) are isomorphic modulo meager sets, which implies that they admit Baire-measurable solutions to exactly the same LCL problems.22 2 The statement in [Wei00] is for zero-dimensional spaces only. The result for general Polish spaces follows since every Polish space contains a comeager zero-dimensional subspace. Thus, we may without loss of generality restrict our attention to a specific choice of a Polish space XX, say X=2X=2, and give the following definition:

When Γ\Gamma is a free group, a version of Theorem 1.10 for the class 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma) does hold:

Theorem 1.13 ([Bra+22, Prop. 6.1, Prop. 6.4, and proof of Thm. 6.6]33 3 Technically, the proof of [Bra+22, Thm. 6.6] is presented for the group (ℤ/2​ℤ)∗n(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{*n} rather than 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}, but exactly the same arguments apply in the 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} case. (The only relevant feature of the group is that its Cayley graph is a tree.) ).

For all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we have

𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)=𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(𝔽n).\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\,=\,\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{F}_{n}).

On the other hand, we show that an analogous statement for the group ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} with n⩾2n\geqslant 2 fails; this is the first known instance where the shift action is not “universal” for Baire-measurable solutions to LCL problems (on any finitely generated group, not just ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}).

The role of shift actions in the context of 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma) is the topic of the next subsection.

1.3.  (Finitary) factors of i.i.d.

We view the unit interval [0,1][0,1] as a probability space with the usual Lebesgue measure. (This is just a concrete example of an atomless standard probability space, which are all isomorphic [Kec95, Thm. 17.41].) The study of measurable functions on 𝒮⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{S}([0,1],\Gamma) (with respect to the product measure) is an important topic in probability theory and ergodic theory, known as the theory of factors of i.i.d. processes44 4 Here “i.i.d.” stands for “independent and identically distributed,” referring to the random variables x⁡(γ)x(\gamma) for γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma and xx drawn at random from 𝒮⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{S}([0,1],\Gamma).. A significant place in this theory is occupied by so-called finitary functions. Since we prefer to work with free actions, we define finitary functions on ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma).

Definition 1.15 (Finitary functions).

Let Γ\Gamma be a finitely generated group and let Λ\Lambda be a finite set. We say that two elements xx, x′∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) agree on a subset D⊆ΓD\subseteq\Gamma if x​(γ)=x′​(γ)x(\gamma)=x^{\prime}(\gamma) for all γ∈D\gamma\in D. A measurable function f:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda is finitary if for almost every x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma), there exists a finite set Dx⊆ΓD_{x}\subseteq\Gamma such that f⁡(x)=f⁡(x′)f(x)=f(x^{\prime}) whenever x′∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) agrees with xx on DxD_{x}.

Holroyd, Schramm, and Wilson [HSW17] initiated the study of LCL problems that can be solved by finitary functions. This line of research was continued in the works of Holroyd [Hol17], Brandt, Hirvonen, Korhonen, Lempiäinen, Östergård, Purcell, Rybicki, Suomela, and Uznańsk [Bra+17], Spinka [Spi20], Brandt, Chang, Grebík, Grunau, Rozhoň, and Vidnyánszky [Bra+22], Grebík and Rozhoň [GR23], and Bencs, Hrušková, and Tóth [BHT24]. Following Grebík and Rozhoň [GR23], we define the following two complexity classes:

Clearly, 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)⊆𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma) and 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)⊆𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma) for every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma. A natural question is whether any of these three classes can be different (see, e.g., [Bra+22, GR23]). For instance, for Γ=ℤ\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}, they coincide [GR21]:

𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤ)=𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤ)=𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤ).\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z})\,=\,\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z})\,=\,\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}).

On the other hand, there exist finitely generated groups Γ\Gamma with 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)≠𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma)\neq\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma); in other words, for such Γ\Gamma, there is an LCL problem Π\Pi such that Π∈𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\Pi\in\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma) but Π∉𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\Pi\notin\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma) (notice the analogy with Theorem 1.14). This fact was recently observed by Kun for the group Γ=(ℤ/2​ℤ)∗d\Gamma=(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{\ast d} with d⩾3d\geqslant 3 in his breakthrough paper [Kun21]. Specifically, Kun proved that the so-called balanced orientation problem is not in 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡((ℤ/2​ℤ)∗d)\mathtt{MEASURE}((\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{\ast d}) [Kun21, Corl. 1.6]; on the other hand, it is in 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡((ℤ/2​ℤ)∗d)\mathtt{FIID}((\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{\ast d}) by a result of Thornton [Tho22]. An alternative construction is to take Γ=(ℤ/d​ℤ)∗(ℤ/d​ℤ)\Gamma=(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})\ast(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}) for d⩾3d\geqslant 3 and let Π\Pi be the problem asking to assign labels 00 and 11 so that exactly one point from each (ℤ/d​ℤ)(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})-orbit gets a 11. It is not hard to see that this is equivalent to finding a perfect matching in an auxiliary dd-regular acyclic graph. As a consequence, Π∈𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡((ℤ/d​ℤ)∗(ℤ/d​ℤ))\Pi\in\mathtt{FIID}((\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})\ast(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})) by a theorem of Lyons and Nazarov [LN11] and Π∉𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡((ℤ/d​ℤ)∗(ℤ/d​ℤ))\Pi\notin\mathtt{MEASURE}((\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})\ast(\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z})) due to [Kun21, Thm. 1.2]. In view of these constructions, it seems very plausible that 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(𝔽n)≠𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\neq\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) for any n⩾2n\geqslant 2, but this is still an open problem. Similarly, it is not known whether 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})=\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) for n⩾2n\geqslant 2.

As for the relationship between 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma) and 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma), it has been poorly understood prior to this work; indeed, the following has been an open question [GPT23, GR23]:

Question 1.17.

Do we have 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)=𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma)=\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma) for every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma?

The class 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma) can be further stratified by measuring the sizes of the sets DxD_{x} appearing in Definition 1.15 [HSW17], and this stratification largely parallels the complexity hierarchy arising in distributed computing [GR23, Bra+22]. Thus, a positive answer to Question 1.17 would establish a close link between distributed algorithms on the one hand and ergodic theory and probability theory on the other. We remark that there exist measurable functions on ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) that are not finitary, but this on its own does not solve Question 1.17 since an LCL problem with a non-finitary measurable solution may also have a different solution that is finitary.

Here we give a negative answer to Question 1.17 for Γ=ℤn\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{n} with n⩾2n\geqslant 2. In fact, we show that the class 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is distinct from both 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}):

As mentioned above, we still do not know whether 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})=\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}).

Another intriguing open question concerns the relationship between the classes 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}). Currently, neither of the inclusions 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)⊆𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subseteq\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)⊆𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subseteq\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is ruled out. That being said, we do have the following:

The proof of Theorem 1.19 relies on the general analysis of the Baire-measurable combinatorics of ℱ⁡(2,Γ)\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma) performed in [Ber21] by the second named author. In the case Γ=ℤn\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{n} with n⩾2n\geqslant 2, the inclusion 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)⊊𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subsetneq\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is strict (see Theorem 1.24 below).

Remark 1.20.

The reader may be wondering why we only define measurable finitary functions and do not introduce versions of Definition 1.15 in the Borel and Baire-measurable contexts. The reason is that such an extension of Definition 1.15 would yield no new complexity classes. Indeed, let us for simplicity consider the space ℱ⁡(2,Γ)\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma) in place of ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma), and say that a Borel (or Baire-measurable) function f:ℱ⁡(2,Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma)\to\Lambda is Borel-finitary (resp. Baire-finitary) if for every point (resp. for a comeager set of points) x∈ℱ⁡(2,Γ)x\in\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma), there exists a finite set Dx⊆ΓD_{x}\subseteq\Gamma such that f⁡(x)=f⁡(x′)f(x)=f(x^{\prime}) whenever x′∈ℱ⁡(2,Γ)x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma) agrees with xx on DxD_{x}. It is not hard to see that a function f:ℱ⁡(2,Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}(2,\Gamma)\to\Lambda is Borel-finitary if and only if it is continuous (this is essentially the definition of the product topology on 𝒮⁡(2,Γ)\mathcal{S}(2,\Gamma)), and every Baire-measurable function is equal to some continuous, hence Baire-finitary function on a comeager set [Tse22, Prop. 9.8]. Note that, in particular, this observation yields the inclusion 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(Γ)⊆𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma).

1.4.  Computable combinatorics

Another way to gauge the complexity of LCL problems is by using computability theory instead of descriptive set theory. This avenue of research has a long history dating back to the 1970s and 1980s; see the survey [Gas98] by Gasarch for an overview. Qian and the fourth named author recently discovered parallels between the computable setting and descriptive combinatorics [QW22], making computable combinatorics part of the general theory of local complexity. In the following definition, we say that an action of a group Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X on a computable set X⊆ℕX\subseteq\mathbb{N} is computable if for each γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma, the function X→X:x↦γ⋅xX\to X:x\mapsto\gamma\cdot x is computable.

Note that if a finitely generated group Γ\Gamma admits a free computable action Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X and X≠∅X\neq\varnothing, then the word problem on Γ\Gamma is decidable: To decide whether σ1⋯σk=𝟏\sigma_{1}\cdots\sigma_{k}=\mathbf{1} for a tuple of generators (σ1,…,σk)(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}), we take any x∈Xx\in X, compute (σ1⋯σk)⋅x(\sigma_{1}\cdots\sigma_{k})\cdot x, and compare the result with xx. Therefore, if the word problem on Γ\Gamma is undecidable, the class 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma) vacuously includes all LCL problems on Γ\Gamma. In other words, Definition 1.21 is only interesting when Γ\Gamma has a decidable word problem, and we shall make this assumption throughout this section.

Although Definitions 1.5 and 1.21 consider rather different types of group actions (Borel vs. computable), it turns out that every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma satisfies the following inclusion:

𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(Γ)⊆𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ).\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\Gamma)\,\subseteq\,\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma).

This is a consequence of [Wei24, Thm. 1.4.1] and [Ber23a, Thm. 1.15]. An interesting question is to determine how the class 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma) relates to 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BOREL}(\Gamma), 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma), and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma). The fourth named author proved [Wei22, Thm. 4]55 5 Technically, [Wei22, Thm. 4] is a result for LCL problems on so-called highly computable regular trees, but the arguments easily transfer to the setting of computable 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}-actions. that for the free group 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n},

𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(𝔽n)=𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n).\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{F}_{n})\,=\,\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}).

Furthermore, various problems have been shown to belong to both 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma) and 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma) for quite general classes of groups Γ\Gamma, often with similar techniques; compare, e.g., [Kie81, Thm. 4.1] and [QW22, Corl. 1.5], [Sch82] and [CMT16], or [Sch80] and [CM16, Wei22a]. In view of these facts, the following question appears natural:

Question 1.22.

Do the classes 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma) and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma) coincide for every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma with a decidable word problem?

We give a negative answer to this question for Γ=ℤn\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{n} with n⩾2n\geqslant 2:

We do not know whether the opposite inclusion 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)⊆𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subseteq\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) holds; indeed, it could even be that 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)⊆𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma) for every finitely generated group Γ\Gamma. We remark that there do exist natural combinatorial problems that can be solved Baire-measurably but not computably. Namely, Manaster and Rosenstein [MR73] constructed, for each d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, a computable dd-regular bipartite graph with no computable perfect matching. On the other hand, Bowen, Conley, and the fourth named author [BCW24] showed that when dd is odd, every Borel dd-regular bipartite graph on a Polish space has a Baire-measurable perfect matching. Unfortunately, the graphs constructed by Manaster and Rosenstein are not generated by free group actions, so they do not directly shed any light on the relationship between the classes 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\Gamma) and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\Gamma).

1.5.  Summary, further results, and an overview of the remainder of the paper

All the results mentioned above, with the exception of Theorem 1.19, follow from the existence of a single LCL problem Π\Pi:

It is clear that Theorem 1.24 implies Theorems 1.8, 1.14, 1.18, and 1.23. The main challenge in proving Theorem 1.24 is to achieve the desired behavior with a locally checkable problem. For example, a version of Theorem 1.14 (non-universality of the shift in the Baire-measurable context) for non-local problems was proved before in [Ber21, Corl. 2.12]; however, that result holds for arbitrary countably infinite groups, which shows that the subtle distinctions between, say, ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} are lost when non-local problems are considered.

The starting point for our construction is a type of combinatorial structure called a toast. This concept originates in the work of Conley and Miller [CM16] (the term “toast” was coined by Miller) and has been widely used in descriptive combinatorics ever since [BKS21, BPZ24, Bra+22, Gao+18, Gao+24, Gao+22, MU17]. Related notions also appear in the theory of random processes [BHT24, HSW17, Spi20]. Recently, Grebík and Rozhoň initiated a systematic study of toast-based constructions, under the name of TOAST algorithms [GR23], and closely related ASI algorithms were studied by Qian and the fourth named author [QW22]. A central role in our arguments is played by toasts with rectangular pieces, which we simply call rectangular toasts. Briefly, a rectangle in a free action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a set of the form R⋅xR\cdot x, where x∈Xx\in X and R⊂ℤnR\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} is an nn-dimensional axis-parallel rectangle in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}, and a rectangular toast ℛ\mathcal{R} for the action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a nested family of rectangles (see Fig. 3). We formally define rectangular toasts and establish their relevant properties in §2. It turns out that one can always construct Borel rectangular toasts ℛ\mathcal{R} such that the union of the rectangles in ℛ\mathcal{R} is conull (Proposition 2.6), but it may be impossible to make it comeager (Proposition 2.12). In other words, building a rectangular toast with a large union is a problem that can be solved measurably but not Baire-measurably, indicating that rectangular toasts may be employed toward proving Theorem 1.8. Unfortunately, the definition of a rectangular toast is plainly non-local. Nevertheless, in §3, we find a way to incorporate rectangular toasts in an LCL problem and show that the resulting problem witnesses Theorem 1.24.

The LCL problem we use to prove Theorem 1.24 can be enhanced with extra layers of structure to derive further separation results between different complexity classes. In particular, in §4 we modify the problem witnessing Theorem 1.24 to obtain the following:

It follows that we have 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(ℤn)⊈𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\not\subseteq\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), and hence 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(ℤn)⊈𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\not\subseteq\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}). Theorem 1.25 also makes a first step toward refuting the possibility that 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is a subset of 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), since it yields an LCL problem that is in 𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) but not in 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}).

We conclude the paper with the proof of Theorem 1.19 in §5 and then some final remarks, including a list of open problems, in §6.

The method of adding extra structure to the LCL problem from Theorem 1.24 that we use to establish Theorem 1.25 is very flexible and can be employed to obtain a variety of other results. Specifically, in the forthcoming second part of this study [Ber+], we will prove the following:

Theorem 1.26 ([Ber+]).

For every integer n⩾2n\geqslant 2, the classes 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), 𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), and 𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) are pairwise incomparable with respect to inclusion.

Although the proof of Theorem 1.26 builds on the work in this paper, it requires a considerable amount of additional technical machinery to be developed; that is why we decided to present it separately. Theorem 1.26 clearly strengthens Theorem 1.8 (since 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is a strict subset of 𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})). In view of the inclusion 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)⊂𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subset\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) (Theorem 1.19), it also strengthens Theorem 1.18. The incomparability between the three classes in Theorem 1.26 makes the contrast between the groups ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n} especially stark, since for the free group 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}, the complexity classes defined in this paper—with the possible exception of 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{F}_{n})—are linearly ordered by inclusion. Theorem 1.26 also shows that, while 𝙲𝙾𝙽𝚃𝙸𝙽𝚄𝙾𝚄𝚂⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{CONTINUOUS}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is the minimum element in the poset of the complexity classes studied in this paper, it does not have a maximum element. (By contrast, for 𝔽n\mathbb{F}_{n}, the class 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)=𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(𝔽n)=𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{F}_{n})=\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{F}_{n})=\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) is maximum.)

The current state of our knowledge regarding the complexity classes of LCL problems on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} for n⩾2n\geqslant 2, including the results of this paper and those of [Ber+], is summarized in Fig. 1.

2.  Rectangular toasts

2.1.  Basic definitions

For the remainder of the paper, we fix an integer n⩾2n\geqslant 2. Before stating the definition of a toast, we need some additional terminology. We shall only define toasts for ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-actions, although the definition can be easily generalized to other structures. For γ\gamma, δ∈ℤn\delta\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, we write 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(γ,δ)≔‖γ−δ‖1\mathsf{dist}(\gamma,\delta)\coloneqq\|\gamma-\delta\|_{1}. Similarly, if ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} on a set XX and xx, y∈Xy\in X are in the same ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-orbit, then there is a unique element γ∈ℤn\gamma\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} such that γ⋅x=y\gamma\cdot x=y, and we let 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,y)≔‖γ‖1\mathsf{dist}(x,y)\coloneqq\|\gamma\|_{1}. If xx and yy are in distinct ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-orbits, we set 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,y)≔∞\mathsf{dist}(x,y)\coloneqq\infty. Note that 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍\mathsf{dist} is an (extended) metric on XX.66 6 As a word of caution, when XX is a Polish space, the topology on XX is induced by a metric, but that metric is different from 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍\mathsf{dist} (unless XX is countable and discrete). We say xx, y∈Xy\in X are adjacent if 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,y)=1\mathsf{dist}(x,y)=1. As usual, for x∈Xx\in X and AA, B⊆XB\subseteq X, we let

𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍(x,A)≔inf{𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍(x,a):a∈A}and𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍(A,B)≔inf{𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍(a,b):a∈A,b∈B}.\mathsf{dist}(x,A)\,\coloneqq\,\inf\{\mathsf{dist}(x,a)\,:\,a\in A\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathsf{dist}(A,B)\,\coloneqq\,\inf\{\mathsf{dist}(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}.

The boundary of A⊆XA\subseteq X is the set ∂A\partial A of all a∈Aa\in A such that 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(a,X∖A)=1\mathsf{dist}(a,X\setminus A)=1. We write [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} to denote the set of all finite subsets of XX.

Definition 2.1 (Toasts).

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} on a set XX. A family 𝒯⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{T}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} of finite sets is a qq-toast, where q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, if the following two conditions hold:

  1. (T1)

    for all KK, L∈𝒯L\in\mathcal{T}, either K∩L=∅K\cap L=\varnothing, or K⊆LK\subseteq L, or L⊆KL\subseteq K, and

  2. (T2)

    for distinct KK, L∈𝒯L\in\mathcal{T}, we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂K,∂L)>q\mathsf{dist}(\partial K,\partial L)>q.

A set K∈𝒯K\in\mathcal{T} is called a piece of the qq-toast 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The boundary of a qq-toast 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the set ∂𝒯≔⋃K∈𝒯∂K\partial\mathcal{T}\coloneqq\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal{T}}\partial K. A qq-toast 𝒯\mathcal{T} is complete77 7 Usually completeness is treated as part of the requirements for being a qq-toast. However, it will be more convenient for us to define it separately. if ⋃𝒯=X\bigcup\mathcal{T}=X, i.e., if for all x∈Xx\in X, there is K∈𝒯K\in\mathcal{T} with x∈Kx\in K. See Fig. 2 for an illustration in the n=2n=2 case.

If XX is a standard Borel space, then the set [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} of all finite subsets of XX also carries a natural standard Borel structure; namely, a subset of [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} is Borel if and only if its preimage in ⨆k=0∞Xk\bigsqcup_{k=0}^{\infty}X^{k} under the map (x0,…,xk−1)↦{x0,…,xk−1}(x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1})\mapsto\{x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1}\} is Borel (see, e.g., [BW23, §2.1]). We say that a family 𝒯\mathcal{T} of finite subsets of XX (for example, a qq-toast) is Borel if it is a Borel subset of [X]<∞{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}. Note that if ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free Borel action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and 𝒯⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{T}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} is a Borel qq-toast, then every element x∈Xx\in X may belong to only countably many pieces K∈𝒯K\in\mathcal{T}. By the Luzin–Novikov uniformization theorem [Kec95, Thm. 18.10], it follows that the sets ⋃𝒯\bigcup\mathcal{T} and ∂𝒯\partial\mathcal{T} are Borel.

The following fundamental fact was established by Gao, Jackson, Krohne, and Seward:

Theorem 2.2 (Gao–Jackson–Krohne–Seward [Gao+24, Corl. 4.13]).

If ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free Borel action on a standard Borel space, then for each q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a Borel complete qq-toast 𝒯⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{T}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}.

We approach Theorem 1.24 by studying qq-toasts with additional constraints on the shapes of their pieces. Specifically, we consider qq-toasts all of whose pieces are nn-dimensional rectangles. We use [a,b][a,b] to denote the closed interval from aa to bb in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, i.e., [a,b]≔{c∈ℤ:a⩽c⩽b}[a,b]\coloneqq\{c\in\mathbb{Z}\,:\,a\leqslant c\leqslant b\}.

Definition 2.3 (Rectangles and rectangular toasts).

A rectangle in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is a set of the form

[a1,b1]×⋯×[an,bn],[a_{1},b_{1}]\times\cdots\times[a_{n},b_{n}],

where a1⩽b1a_{1}\leqslant b_{1}, …, an⩽bna_{n}\leqslant b_{n} are integers. The values bi−aib_{i}-a_{i} for 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n are called the side lengths of the rectangle. A rectangle all of whose side lengths are equal (to NN) is called an (NN-)square.

Given a free action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, a subset of XX is a rectangle (resp. a square) if it has the form R⋅x≔{γ⋅x:γ∈R}R\cdot x\coloneqq\{\gamma\cdot x\,:\,\gamma\in R\} for a point x∈Xx\in X and a rectangle (resp. a square) R⊂ℤnR\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n}. The side lengths of R⋅xR\cdot x are those of RR. A rectangular (resp. square) qq-toast is a qq-toast all of whose pieces are rectangles (resp. squares) with side lengths at least qq. See Fig. 3 for an illustration in the n=2n=2 case.

Remark 2.4.

Since we are assuming that n⩾2n\geqslant 2, if KK, LL are two rectangles with ∂K∩∂L≠∅\partial K\cap\partial L\neq\varnothing, then either K∩L=∅K\cap L=\varnothing, or K⊂LK\subset L, or L⊂KL\subset K. Hence, when 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a set of rectangles, condition (T2) in Definition 2.1 implies (T1).

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and let ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} be a rectangular qq-toast. An important role in our arguments will be played by the points of XX whose entire ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-orbit is covered by ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R}. That is, we say that a point x∈Xx\in X is ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete if ℤn⋅x⊆⋃ℛ\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot x\subseteq\bigcup\mathcal{R}. Equivalently, x∈Xx\in X is ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete if x∉ℤn⋅(X∖⋃ℛ)x\notin\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot(X\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R}). The following simple observation will be helpful:

Lemma 2.5.

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and let ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} be a rectangular qq-toast for some q⩾1q\geqslant 1. If x∈Xx\in X is an ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete point, then each y∈ℤn⋅xy\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot x is contained in infinitely many pieces of ℛ\mathcal{R}, and the set ℤn⋅x\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot x includes pieces of ℛ\mathcal{R} all of whose side lengths are arbitrarily large.

Proof.

It suffices to show that for each rectangle K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} with K⊆ℤn⋅xK\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot x, there exists another rectangle K′∈ℛK^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} such that K′⊋KK^{\prime}\supsetneq K (which implies that every side length of K′K^{\prime} strictly exceeds the corresponding side length of KK). To this end, take a point y∉Ky\notin K adjacent to the boundary of KK and note that any rectangle K′∈ℛK^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} containing yy must satisfy K′⊋KK^{\prime}\supsetneq K. ∎

In §§2.2–2.6 we present a series of facts about rectangular toasts used to prove Theorem 1.24.

2.2.  Rectangular toasts and measure theory

We start by showing that every free Borel action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} admits a square qq-toast that is “almost” complete from the point of view of measure theory.

Proposition 2.6.

Let ℤn⮌(X,μ)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}(X,\mu) be a free Borel action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} on a standard probability space (X,μ)(X,\mu). Then for each q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a Borel square qq-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} with μ⁡(⋃ℛ)=1\mu(\bigcup\mathcal{R})=1.

This statement seems well known to experts in the area, although we were unable to find a proof in the literature. For completeness, we prove it here. First we need to review some concepts from the theory of Borel graphs. A graph GG is Borel if its vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) is a standard Borel space and its edge set E⁡(G)E(G) is a Borel subset of [V⁡(G)]2{[{V(G)}]^{2}}. (Here we write [V⁡(G)]2⊂[V⁡(G)]<∞{[{V(G)}]^{2}}\subset{[{{V(G)}}]^{{<\infty}}} for the set of all 22-element subsets of V⁡(G)V(G).) Borel graphs are the main objects of study in descriptive combinatorics; see [KM20, Pik21] for an overview.

A subgraph of a graph GG is a graph HH such that V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) and E⁡(H)⊆E⁡(G)E(H)\subseteq E(G). We write H⊆GH\subseteq G to mean that HH is a subgraph of GG. If GG and HH are Borel graphs and V⁡(H)⊆V⁡(G)V(H)\subseteq V(G) is a Borel set equipped with the relative Borel σ\sigma-algebra, then we call HH a Borel subgraph of GG.

Definition 2.7 (Hyperfinite graphs).

A graph GG is component-finite if every connected component of GG is finite. A Borel graph GG is hyperfinite if there is an increasing sequence G0⊆G1⊆⋯⊆GG_{0}\subseteq G_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq G of component-finite Borel subgraphs of GG whose union is GG.

The systematic study of hyperfinite graphs was initiated by Weiss [Wei84] and Slaman and Steel [SS88], with important foundational work done by Dougherty, Jackson, and Kechris [DJK94] and Jackson, Kechris, and Louveau [JKL02], among others. For an overview of this topic, see [Kec23]. We shall use the following fact:

Theorem 2.8 (Weiss (unpublished); see [JKL02]).

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free Borel action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} on a standard Borel space XX and let 𝟎∉S⊆ℤn\bm{0}\notin S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n} be a finite subset. If GG is the graph with vertex set XX and edge set E(G)≔{{x,σ⋅x}:x∈X,σ∈S}E(G)\coloneqq\{\{x,\sigma\cdot x\}\,:\,x\in X,\,\sigma\in S\}, then GG is hyperfinite.

We remark that Theorem 2.8 is a corollary of Theorem 2.2, since the existence of a Borel 11-toast implies hyperfiniteness [Gao+24]. A long-standing open question raised by Weiss is whether a version of Theorem 2.8 holds for every amenable countable group in place of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} [Wei84]; for partial results see [JKL02] by Jackson, Kechris, and Louveau and [Con+23] by Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward, and Tucker-Drob. However, if null sets are ignored (as indeed they are in this subsection), Weiss’s question has a positive answer due to Ornstein and Weiss [OW80].

A set I⊆V⁡(G)I\subseteq V(G) is independent in a graph GG if no two vertices in II are adjacent. The chromatic number χ⁡(G)\chi(G) of GG is the minimum k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} (if it exists) such that V⁡(G)V(G) can be covered by kk independent sets; if there is no such kk, we set χ⁡(G)≔∞\chi(G)\coloneqq\infty. Equivalently, χ⁡(G)\chi(G) is the least kk such that GG has a proper kk-coloring, i.e., a labeling f:V⁡(G)→kf\colon V(G)\to k such that adjacent vertices receive different labels (we have already discussed this concept in Example 1.2). The chromatic number of a graph is of fundamental importance in graph theory; see [JT95, Cra24] for an overview. Naturally, it is also central to the study of Borel graphs [KST99]. For a Borel graph GG and a probability Borel measure μ\mu on V⁡(G)V(G), the μ\mu-approximate chromatic number χμ𝖺𝗉​(G)\chi_{\mu}^{\mathsf{ap}}(G) of GG is the minimum k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} (if it exists) such that for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we can find Borel independent sets I1I_{1}, …, Ik⊆V⁡(G)I_{k}\subseteq V(G) with μ⁡(I1∪…∪Ik)⩾1−ε\mu(I_{1}\cup\ldots\cup I_{k})\geqslant 1-\varepsilon. A graph GG is locally finite if every vertex of GG has finitely many neighbors. We shall use the following result of Conley and Kechris:

Theorem 2.9 (Conley–Kechris [CK13, Thm. 3.8]).

If GG is a locally finite hyperfinite Borel graph and μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G), then χμ𝖺𝗉​(G)⩽χ⁡(G)\chi_{\mu}^{\mathsf{ap}}(G)\leqslant\chi(G).

The following lemma is a consequence of Theorems 2.8 and 2.9. For measure-preserving actions, it essentially follows from the Ornstein–Weiss construction of quasi-tilings, cf. [OW87, Thm. 5].

Lemma 2.10.

Let ℤn⮌(X,μ)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}(X,\mu) be a free Borel action on a standard probability space. For all q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist N=N⁡(n,q,ε)∈ℕN=N(n,q,\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{N} (depending only on nn, qq, and ε\varepsilon but not on the action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X or the measure μ\mu) and a Borel set 𝒟⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{D}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} of NN-squares such that N⩾qN\geqslant q and:

  • —

    μ⁡(⋃𝒟)⩾1−ε\mu(\bigcup\mathcal{D})\geqslant 1-\varepsilon, and

  • —

    for distinct CC, D∈𝒟D\in\mathcal{D}, we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(C,D)>q\mathsf{dist}(C,D)>q.

Proof.

Fix r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} and ε>0\varepsilon>0 and let N⩾qN\geqslant q be a large natural number to be determined later. Define a new probability measure ν\nu on XX by the formula

ν⁡(A)≔1(N+1)n​∑δ∈[0,N]nμ⁡(δ⋅A).\nu(A)\,\coloneqq\,\frac{1}{(N+1)^{n}}\sum_{\delta\in[0,N]^{n}}\mu(\delta\cdot A).

(Note that if the action ℤn⮌(X,μ)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}(X,\mu) is measure-preserving, then ν=μ\nu=\mu.) Let GG be the graph with vertex set XX and edge set

E⁡(G)≔{{x,y}∈[X]2:x≠y​ and ​𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍​([0,N]n⋅x,[0,N]n⋅y)⩽q}.E(G)\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\{x,y\}\in{[{X}]^{2}}\,:\,x\neq y\text{ and }\mathsf{dist}([0,N]^{n}\cdot x,\,[0,N]^{n}\cdot y)\,\leqslant\,q\big\}.

By Theorem 2.8 applied with

S≔{γ∈ℤn:γ≠0​ and ​𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍​([0,N]n,[0,N]n+γ)⩽q},S\,\coloneqq\,\{\gamma\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\,:\,\gamma\neq 0\text{ and }\mathsf{dist}([0,N]^{n},\,[0,N]^{n}+\gamma)\,\leqslant\,q\},

the graph GG is hyperfinite. Therefore, by Theorem 2.9, χν𝖺𝗉​(G)⩽χ⁡(G)\chi^{\mathsf{ap}}_{\nu}(G)\leqslant\chi(G). Note that each connected component of GG is isomorphic to the Cayley graph 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤn,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}^{n},S), and hence χ⁡(G)=χ⁡(𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤn,S))\chi(G)=\chi(\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}^{n},S)). The graph 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤn,S)\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}^{n},S) can be partitioned into k≔(N+q+1)nk\coloneqq(N+q+1)^{n} independent sets, namely

Iη≔(N+q+1)​ℤn+η,for each ​η∈[0,N+q]n.I_{\eta}\,\coloneqq\,(N+q+1)\mathbb{Z}^{n}+\eta,\quad\text{for each }\eta\in[0,N+q]^{n}.

Therefore, χ⁡(𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤn,S))⩽k\chi(\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}^{n},S))\leqslant k.88 8 In fact, χ⁡(𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤn,S))=k\chi(\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}^{n},S))=k, but we only need the upper bound. It follows that χν𝖺𝗉​(G)⩽k\chi^{\mathsf{ap}}_{\nu}(G)\leqslant k. Therefore, there exist Borel independent sets I1I_{1}, …, Ik⊆XI_{k}\subseteq X in GG such that ν⁡(I1∪…∪Ik)⩾1−ε/2\nu(I_{1}\cup\ldots\cup I_{k})\geqslant 1-\varepsilon/2. Let II be the set among I1I_{1}, …, IkI_{k} whose ν\nu-measure is maximum. Then ν⁡(I)⩾(1−ε/2)/k\nu(I)\geqslant(1-\varepsilon/2)/k. We claim that the following set 𝒟\mathcal{D} of NN-squares satisfies the requirements of the lemma:

𝒟≔{[0,N]n⋅x:x∈I}.\mathcal{D}\,\coloneqq\,\{[0,N]^{n}\cdot x\,:\,x\in I\}.

Since II is independent in GG, distinct CC, D∈𝒟D\in\mathcal{D} satisfy 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(C,D)>q\mathsf{dist}(C,D)>q, as desired. It remains to compute a lower bound on μ⁡(⋃𝒟)\mu(\bigcup\mathcal{D}). To this end, we observe that

⋃𝒟=[0,N]n⋅I=⋃δ∈[0,N]n(δ⋅I).\bigcup\mathcal{D}\,=\,[0,N]^{n}\cdot I\,=\,\bigcup_{\delta\in[0,N]^{n}}(\delta\cdot I).

Thus, as the sets δ⋅I\delta\cdot I for δ∈[0,N]n\delta\in[0,N]^{n} are pairwise disjoint, we have

μ⁡(⋃𝒟)=∑δ∈[0,N]nμ⁡(δ⋅I)=(N+1)n​ν​(I)⩾(N+1N+q+1)n​(1−ε/2)⩾ 1−ε,\mu\left(\bigcup\mathcal{D}\right)\,=\,\sum_{\delta\in[0,N]^{n}}\mu(\delta\cdot I)\,=\,(N+1)^{n}\,\nu(I)\,\geqslant\,\left(\frac{N+1}{N+q+1}\right)^{n}\,(1-\varepsilon/2)\,\geqslant\,1-\varepsilon,

where the last inequality holds for all NN large enough as a function of nn, qq, and ε\varepsilon, as desired. ∎

    νi​(⋃𝒟i)⩾1−εi\nu_{i}(\bigcup\mathcal{D}_{i})\geqslant 1-\varepsilon_{i}, and

    for distinct CC, D∈𝒟iD\in\mathcal{D}_{i}, we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(C,D)>q\mathsf{dist}(C,D)>q.

2.3.  Rectangular toasts and Baire category

Gao, Jackson, Krohne, and Seward showed [Gao+22, Thm. 1.6] that the loss of a null set in Proposition 2.6 is necessary, that is, a free Borel action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} may not have a Borel complete rectangular 11-toast.99 9 The arguments in [Gao+22] are for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, but the generalization to ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is straightforward. Note that this crucially uses the assumption that n⩾2n\geqslant 2 (and fails for n=1n=1). Their obstruction is Baire-categorical in nature; they construct a certain profinite action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and show that ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} cannot be comeager for any Borel rectangular 11-toast ℛ\mathcal{R} on this action. Here we observe that this conclusion actually holds for a rather general class of actions.

Definition 2.11 (Minimal actions).

Let Γ⮌X\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a continuous action of a group Γ\Gamma on a compact space XX. The action of γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma on XX is minimal if for every x∈Xx\in X, the set {γk⋅x:k∈ℕ}\{\gamma^{k}\cdot x\,:\,k\in\mathbb{N}\} is dense.

In the following, we let 𝖾1\mathsf{e}_{1}, …, 𝖾n\mathsf{e}_{n} be the standard generators of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}.

Proposition 2.12.

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free continuous action on a compact Polish space X≠∅X\neq\varnothing. If the action of 𝖾1\mathsf{e}_{1} is minimal, then for any Borel rectangular 11-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}, ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is not comeager.

For a concrete example of such an action, take X=𝕊1X=\mathbb{S}^{1}, the circle. For α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}, let Tα:𝕊1→𝕊1T_{\alpha}\colon\mathbb{S}^{1}\to\mathbb{S}^{1} be the rotation by the angle 2​π​α2\pi\alpha. Fix ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linearly independent numbers α1\alpha_{1}, …, αn∈ℝ∖ℚ\alpha_{n}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q} and define

(k1,…,kn)⋅x≔Tk1​α1+⋯+kn​αn​(x)for all ​(k1,…,kn)∈ℤn​ and ​x∈𝕊1.(k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})\cdot x\,\coloneqq\,T_{k_{1}\alpha_{1}\,+\,\cdots\,+\,k_{n}\alpha_{n}}(x)\quad\text{for all }(k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\text{ and }x\in\mathbb{S}^{1}.

The ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear independence of α1\alpha_{1}, …, αn\alpha_{n} ensures that this action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is free, and since α1∉ℚ\alpha_{1}\notin\mathbb{Q}, the set {Tk​α1​(x):k∈ℕ}\{T_{k\alpha_{1}}(x)\,:\,k\in\mathbb{N}\} is dense for every x∈𝕊1x\in\mathbb{S}^{1} [KH12, Prop. 1.3.3].

Proof of Proposition 2.12.

Note that since the action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is continuous, a Borel set A⊆XA\subseteq X is meager if and only if ℤn⋅A\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot A is meager. Let ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} be a Borel rectangular 11-toast. Since the boundaries of the pieces of ℛ\mathcal{R} are at distance at least 22 from each other, the set D≔X∖∂ℛD\coloneqq X\setminus\partial\mathcal{R} satisfies

D∪⋃i=1n(𝖾i⋅D)∪⋃i=1n((−𝖾i)⋅D)=X.D\,\cup\,\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}(\mathsf{e}_{i}\cdot D)\,\cup\,\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}((-\mathsf{e}_{i})\cdot D)\,=\,X.

It follows that DD is nonmeager. Let U⊆XU\subseteq X be a nonempty open set such that U∖DU\setminus D is meager (which exists by [Tse22, Prop. 9.8]). Since the action of 𝖾1\mathsf{e}_{1} is minimal, we have ⋃k∈ℕ((−k​𝖾1)⋅U)=X\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}((-k\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot U)=X, and the compactness of XX yields an integer N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that ⋃0⩽k⩽N((−k​𝖾1)⋅U)=X\bigcup_{0\leqslant k\leqslant N}((-k\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot U)=X. It follows that the set ⋃0⩽k⩽N((−k​𝖾1)⋅D)\bigcup_{0\leqslant k\leqslant N}((-k\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot D) is comeager, and thus its complement, i.e.,

M≔X∖⋃0⩽k⩽N((−k​𝖾1)⋅D)={y∈X:(k​𝖾1)⋅y∈∂ℛ​ for all ​0⩽k⩽N}M\,\coloneqq\,X\,\setminus\,\bigcup_{0\leqslant k\leqslant N}((-k\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot D)\,=\,\big\{y\in X\,:\,(k\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot y\in\partial\mathcal{R}\text{ for all }0\leqslant k\leqslant N\big\}

is meager. Now suppose that x∈Xx\in X is an ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete point. By Lemma 2.5, the set ℤn⋅x\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot x includes a rectangle K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} all of whose side lengths exceed NN. Since n⩾2n\geqslant 2, there is y∈ℤn⋅xy\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot x such that the boundary of KK contains all of the points yy, 𝖾1⋅y\mathsf{e}_{1}\cdot y, (2​𝖾1)⋅y(2\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot y, …, (N​𝖾1)⋅y(N\mathsf{e}_{1})\cdot y, which implies that y∈My\in M. In other words, the set of all ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete points is a subset of ℤn⋅M\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot M, and hence it is meager. Therefore, the set ℤn⋅(X∖⋃ℛ)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot(X\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R}) is comeager, so X∖⋃ℛX\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R} is nonmeager, as desired. ∎

2.4.  Rectangular toasts and shifts

Our next proposition asserts that the shift action ℤn⮌ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) does not satisfy the conclusion of Proposition 2.12:

Proposition 2.13.

For each q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a Borel square qq-toast ℛ⊆[ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n})}}]^{{<\infty}}} such that the set ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is comeager.

Proof.

Define ρ:ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)→2\rho\colon\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n})\to 2 by ρ⁡(x)≔x⁡(𝟎)\rho(x)\coloneqq x(\bm{0}). Call a square KK in ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) safe if

  • —

    the side length of KK is at least qq, and

  • —

    for all x∈Xx\in X, if x∈∂Kx\in\partial K, then ρ⁡(x)=1\rho(x)=1, and if 0<𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,∂K)⩽q0<\mathsf{dist}(x,\partial K)\leqslant q, then ρ⁡(x)=0\rho(x)=0.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the set of all safe squares. We claim that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a square qq-toast such that ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is comeager, as desired. If KK, L∈ℛL\in\mathcal{R} are two distinct squares, then 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂K,∂L)>q\mathsf{dist}(\partial K,\partial L)>q, because ρ\rho is equal to 11 on ∂K\partial K and 00 on all the elements of X∖∂LX\setminus\partial L at distance at most qq from ∂L\partial L. By Remark 2.4, it follows that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a square qq-toast. It remains to check that ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is comeager.

Note that a point x∈ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) belongs to ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} if and only if there exists a square R⊂ℤnR\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} with side length at least qq such that R∋𝟎R\ni\bm{0} and for all γ∈ℤn\gamma\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},

  • —

    if γ∈∂R\gamma\in\partial R, then x⁡(γ)=1x(\gamma)=1, and

  • —

    if 0<𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(γ,∂R)⩽q0<\mathsf{dist}(\gamma,\partial R)\leqslant q, then x⁡(γ)=0x(\gamma)=0.

In particular, the set ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is open, since the existence of such a square RR is witnessed by the restriction of xx to a finite subset of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}. We claim ∂ℛ\partial\mathcal{R} is dense. Indeed, the topology on ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is generated by clopen sets of the form

US,φ≔{x∈ℱ⁡(2,ℤn):x|S=φ},U_{S,\varphi}\,\coloneqq\,\{x\in\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n})\,:\,{{x}|_{S}}=\varphi\},

where S⊂ℤnS\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} is finite and φ:S→2\varphi\colon S\to 2. Given such a set US,φU_{S,\varphi}, we need to show US,φ∩⋃ℛ≠∅U_{S,\varphi}\cap\bigcup\mathcal{R}\neq\varnothing. Take an arbitrary square RR in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} with side length at least qq, {𝟎}∪S⊂R\{\bm{0}\}\cup S\subset R, and 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(S,∂R)>q\mathsf{dist}(S,\partial R)>q (which exists because SS is a finite set), and define x:ℤn→2x\colon\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to 2 by

x⁡(γ)≔{φ⁡(γ)if ​γ∈S,1if ​γ∈∂R,0otherwise.x(\gamma)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\varphi(\gamma)&\text{if }\gamma\in S,\\ 1&\text{if }\gamma\in\partial R,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Then x∈US,φx\in U_{S,\varphi} and R⋅xR\cdot x is a safe square containing xx, so x∈US,φ∩⋃ℛx\in U_{S,\varphi}\cap\bigcup\mathcal{R}, as desired. This shows that ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is a dense open—hence comeager—set, and the proof is complete. ∎

2.5.  Rectangular toasts and finitary factors of i.i.d.

Before analyzing rectangular toasts from the point of view of finitary factors of i.i.d., it will be helpful to address a certain technical subtlety in Definition 1.15. Notice that if f:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda is equal to a finitary function almost everywhere, then ff itself need not be finitary; however, such ff must have a somewhat weaker property that we call being weakly finitary. To define this notion, we first need to introduce a useful piece of terminology.

Suppose x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) and D⊆ΓD\subseteq\Gamma. The product measure ℒΓ∖D\mathcal{L}^{\Gamma\setminus D} on [0,1]Γ∖D[0,1]^{\Gamma\setminus D} then naturally gives rise to a probability measure on the set of all points x′∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) that agree with xx on DD. When in the sequel we use the phrase “for almost all x′x^{\prime} that agree with xx on DD,” the words “almost all” refer to this measure.

Definition 2.14 (Weakly finitary functions).

Let Γ\Gamma be a finitely generated group and let Λ\Lambda be a finite set. A measurable function f:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda is weakly finitary if for almost every x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma), there exists a finite set Dx⊆ΓD_{x}\subseteq\Gamma such that f⁡(x)=f⁡(x′)f(x)=f(x^{\prime}) for almost all x′∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) that agree with xx on DxD_{x}.

Definition 2.14 differs from Definition 1.15 in that f⁡(x′)f(x^{\prime}) must equal f⁡(x)f(x) for almost all x′x^{\prime} agreeing with xx on DxD_{x}, and not necessarily for all such xx. A straightforward application of Fubini’s theorem shows that if f:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda is weakly finitary (for instance, if ff is finitary) and f′:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda agrees with ff almost everywhere, then f′f^{\prime} is also weakly finitary.

In practice, when working with a measurable function ff, it is often convenient to replace ff by a Borel function f′f^{\prime} that agrees with ff almost everywhere. It is therefore useful to observe that for weakly finitary ff, such f′f^{\prime} can be chosen to be finitary (in the strong sense of Definition 1.15):

Proposition 2.15.

Let Γ\Gamma be a finitely generated group and let Λ\Lambda be a finite set. If f:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda is weakly finitary, then there exists a Borel finitary function f′:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda that is equal to ff almost everywhere.

Proof.

Upon modifying ff on a null set, we may assume that ff is Borel (and still weakly finitary). Fix an increasing sequence (Dk)k∈ℕ(D_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} of finite subsets of Γ\Gamma such that ⋃k∈ℕDk=Γ\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}D_{k}=\Gamma and define f′:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf^{\prime}\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda as follows: If there exist k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and (necessarily unique) λk∈Λ\lambda_{k}\in\Lambda such that f⁡(x′)=λkf(x^{\prime})=\lambda_{k} for almost all x′x^{\prime} that agree with xx on DkD_{k}, then let f′​(x)≔λkf^{\prime}(x)\coloneqq\lambda_{k} for the smallest such kk; otherwise, let f′​(x)f^{\prime}(x) be any fixed element λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda. The function f′f^{\prime} is Borel by [Kec95, Thm. 17.25]. Moreover, since ff is weakly finitary, for almost all xx, there exist DkD_{k} and λk\lambda_{k} as above, and f′​(x′)=f′​(x)=λkf^{\prime}(x^{\prime})=f^{\prime}(x)=\lambda_{k} for all x′x^{\prime} that agree with xx on DkD_{k}. Hence, f′f^{\prime} is finitary. It is also clear from the construction that ff and f′f^{\prime} are equal almost everywhere. ∎

The above proposition will not be explicitly invoked in the sequel, but it explains why we can safely replace “finitary” with the more robust notion of “weakly finitary.”

After these preliminaries, we are ready to show that the square toasts given by Proposition 2.6 applied to ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) must in a certain sense be non-finitary. In the following, we use ℒ\mathcal{L} to denote the Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1].

Proposition 2.16.

Suppose that ℛ⊆[ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})}}]^{{<\infty}}} is a Borel rectangular 11-toast such that ℒℤn​(⋃ℛ)=1\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(\bigcup\mathcal{R})=1. Then the characteristic function of the set ∂ℛ\partial\mathcal{R} is not weakly finitary.

We again stress that Proposition 2.16 relies on the assumption that n⩾2n\geqslant 2.

Proof.

Let f:ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)→{0,1}f\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})\to\{0,1\} be the characteristic function of ∂ℛ\partial\mathcal{R} and suppose for contradiction that it is weakly finitary. For a finite set D⊂ℤnD\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} and a function φ:D→[0,1]\varphi\colon D\to[0,1], we say that φ\varphi weakly determines ff if the value f⁡(x)f(x) is the same for almost all x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) with x|D=φ{{x}|_{D}}=\varphi. Let B⁡(D)⊆[0,1]DB(D)\subseteq[0,1]^{D} be the set of all φ:D→[0,1]\varphi\colon D\to[0,1] that weakly determine ff, and for i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, let Bi​(D)B_{i}(D) be the set of all φ∈B⁡(D)\varphi\in B(D) such that the common value of ff on almost all points extending φ\varphi is ii. The sets B⁡(D)B(D), B0​(D)B_{0}(D), B1​(D)B_{1}(D) are ℒD\mathcal{L}^{D}-measurable by Fubini’s theorem.

Since ff is weakly finitary, for almost all x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}), there is a finite set Dx⊂ℤnD_{x}\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} such that x|Dx{{x}|_{D_{x}}} weakly determines ff and, furthermore,

x|Dx∈Bf⁡(x)​(Dx).{{x}|_{D_{x}}}\,\in\,B_{f(x)}(D_{x}).

Since the boundaries of the pieces of ℛ\mathcal{R} are a distance at least 22 apart, f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 for a set of points x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) of positive measure. As there are only countably many finite subsets of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}, Fubini’s theorem shows that there exists a finite set D⊂ℤnD\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} such that ε≔ℒD​(B0​(D))>0\varepsilon\coloneqq\mathcal{L}^{D}(B_{0}(D))>0.

We shall employ the following simple observation:

Claim 2.17.

If S⊂ℤnS\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} is a finite set, then there exists a subset S′⊆SS^{\prime}\subseteq S of size |S′|⩾|S|/|D|2|S^{\prime}|\geqslant|S|/|D|^{2} such that the sets D+γD+\gamma for γ∈S′\gamma\in S^{\prime} are pairwise disjoint.

Proof.

Let S′⊆SS^{\prime}\subseteq S be a maximal subset such that the sets D+γD+\gamma for γ∈S′\gamma\in S^{\prime} are pairwise disjoint. Then for each γ∈S∖S′\gamma\in S\setminus S^{\prime}, there is γ′∈S′\gamma^{\prime}\in S^{\prime} with (D+γ)∩(D+γ′)≠∅(D+\gamma)\cap(D+\gamma^{\prime})\neq\varnothing, i.e., γ∈D−D+γ′\gamma\in D-D+\gamma^{\prime}. On the other hand, for each γ′∈S′\gamma^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}, there are fewer than |D−D|⩽|D|2|D-D|\leqslant|D|^{2} elements γ∈S∖S′\gamma\in S\setminus S^{\prime} in D−D+γ′D-D+\gamma^{\prime} (note that γ′\gamma^{\prime} itself should not be counted). Thus, (|D|2−1)​|S′|⩾|S|−|S′|(|D|^{2}-1)|S^{\prime}|\geqslant|S|-|S^{\prime}|, i.e., |S′|⩾|S|/|D|2|S^{\prime}|\geqslant|S|/|D|^{2}. ∎

Let x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) be a random point sampled from the distribution ℒℤn\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}} and let Ξ\Xi be the random variable equal to the number of rectangles in ℛ\mathcal{R} that contain xx. We claim that the expectation of Ξ\Xi is finite. Consider a fixed rectangle RR in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} with side lengths N1N_{1}, …, NnN_{n} such that 𝟎∈R\bm{0}\in R. If R⋅x∈ℛR\cdot x\in\mathcal{R}, then for all δ∈∂R\delta\in\partial R, we have f⁡(δ⋅x)=1f(\delta\cdot x)=1, and hence, with probability 1, (δ⋅x)|D∉B0​(D){{(\delta\cdot x)}|_{D}}\notin B_{0}(D). Let S⊆∂RS\subseteq\partial R be a set of size |S|⩾|∂R|/|D|2|S|\geqslant|\partial R|/|D|^{2} such that the sets D+δD+\delta for δ∈S\delta\in S are pairwise disjoint, which exists by Claim 2.17. Then the random events (δ⋅x)|D∉B0​(D){{(\delta\cdot x)}|_{D}}\notin B_{0}(D) for δ∈S\delta\in S are independent, so

ℙ[R⋅x∈ℛ]⩽ℙ[(δ⋅x)|D∉B0(D) for all δ∈S]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[R\cdot x\in\mathcal{R}]\,\leqslant\,\mathbb{P}\big[{{(\delta\cdot x)}|_{D}}\notin B_{0}(D)\text{ for all }\delta\in S\big]\, =(1−ε)|S|\displaystyle=\,(1-\varepsilon)^{|S|}
⩽(1−ε)|∂R|/|D|2⩽∏i=1n(1−ε)Ni/|D|2,\displaystyle\leqslant\,(1-\varepsilon)^{|\partial R|/|D|^{2}}\,\leqslant\,\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-\varepsilon)^{N_{i}/|D|^{2}},

where in the last step we use the crude bound |∂R|⩾∑i=1NNi|\partial R|\geqslant\sum_{i=1}^{N}N_{i}. (This is where the assumption n⩾2n\geqslant 2 is invoked.)
