𝔼[Ξ]=∑Rℙ[R⋅x∈ℛ]⩽∑N1,…,Nn∏i=1n(Ni(1−ε)Ni/|D|2)=(∑N=1∞N(1−ε)N/|D|2)n<∞,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Xi]\,=\,\sum_{R}\mathbb{P}[R\cdot x\in\mathcal{R}]\,\leqslant\,\sum_{N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(N_{i}(1-\varepsilon)^{N_{i}/|D|^{2}}\right)\,=\,\left(\sum_{N=1}^{\infty}N(1-\varepsilon)^{N/|D|^{2}}\right)^{n}\,<\,\infty,

as desired. (Here the first summation is over all rectangles RR in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} containing 𝟎\bm{0}, and the second one is over all integers N1N_{1}, …, Nn⩾1N_{n}\geqslant 1.)

It follows that Ξ<∞\Xi<\infty almost always, i.e., almost every point x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is contained in finitely many rectangles in ℛ\mathcal{R}. By Lemma 2.5, this means that the set of all ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete points is null, i.e., ℒℤn​(ℤn⋅(X∖⋃ℛ))=1\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot(X\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R}))=1. Since the action ℤn⮌ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is measure-preserving, we conclude that the set X∖⋃ℛX\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R} has positive measure, which is a contradiction. ∎

2.6.  Computable rectangular toasts

Now we turn our attention to the computability-theoretic aspects of rectangular toasts. We say that a set ℛ⊆[ℕ]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{\mathbb{N}}}]^{{<\infty}}} is computable if there is an algorithm that, given a tuple (x1,…,xk)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) of natural numbers, decides if {x1,…,xk}∈ℛ\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\in\mathcal{R}. The following proposition was pointed out to us by Riley Thornton in a personal communication as a potential tool for resolving Question 1.22.

Proposition 2.18.

For every free computable action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X on a computable set X⊆ℕX\subseteq\mathbb{N} and for each q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a computable complete square qq-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that X=ℕX=\mathbb{N}. We shall describe an algorithm that enumerates a sequence R0R_{0}, R1R_{1}, … with the following properties:

  1. (R1)

    each RiR_{i} is an NiN_{i}-square in XX for some Ni⩾i+qN_{i}\geqslant i+q,

  2. (R2)

    for all i≠ji\neq j, we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂Ri,∂Rj)>q\mathsf{dist}(\partial R_{i},\partial R_{j})>q,

  3. (R3)

    for all x∈ℕx\in\mathbb{N}, x∈Rxx\in R_{x}.

The set ℛ≔{Ri:i∈ℕ}\mathcal{R}\coloneqq\{R_{i}\,:\,i\in\mathbb{N}\} is a desired computable compete square qq-toast. Indeed, ℛ\mathcal{R} is a square qq-toast by (R1) and (R2), and it is complete by (R3). Furthermore, ℛ\mathcal{R} is computable because, given a tuple (x1,…,xk)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) such that R≔{x1,…,xk}R\coloneqq\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\} is an NN-square, we can decide if RR is in ℛ\mathcal{R} by computing R0R_{0}, …, RNR_{N}. If R=RiR=R_{i} for some 0⩽i⩽N0\leqslant i\leqslant N, then R∈ℛR\in\mathcal{R}; otherwise, R∉ℛR\notin\mathcal{R} by (R1).

To enumerate R0R_{0}, R1R_{1}, …, we proceed as follows. Note that, since the action ℤn⮌ℕ\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathbb{N} is computable, given two rectangles RR and R′R^{\prime}, we can computably determine whether 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂R,∂R′)>q\mathsf{dist}(\partial R,\partial R^{\prime})>q. Assume that R0R_{0}, …, Ri−1R_{i-1} have already been computed. We then cycle through the integers j⩾i+qj\geqslant i+q until we find one such that 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂([−j,j]n⋅i),∂Rt)>q\mathsf{dist}(\partial([-j,j]^{n}\cdot i),\partial R_{t})>q for all t∈{0,…,i−1}t\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}. Note that such jj must exist because the set {R0,…,Ri−1}\{R_{0},\ldots,R_{i-1}\} is finite. We then let Ni≔2​jN_{i}\coloneqq 2j and Ri≔[−j,j]n⋅iR_{i}\coloneqq[-j,j]^{n}\cdot i. This construction clearly satisfies properties (R1)–(R3), as desired. ∎

3.  LCL problems based on rectangular toasts

3.1.  The rectangular qq-toast problem

In view of Propositions 2.6, 2.12, 2.13, 2.16, and 2.18, our goal now is to reduce the task of finding a complete rectangular qq-toast for some q⩾1q\geqslant 1 to solving an LCL problem. The challenge is to “localize” the seemingly “global” notion of a complete rectangular qq-toast. We do this in two steps. First, for each (large enough) qq, we describe an LCL problem 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q) on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} whose solutions encode rectangular qq-toasts (there are some technical caveats to this statement that are discussed below). After that, in §§3.2, 3.3, we explain how to modify the problem to force the rectangular qq-toast to be complete. In the latter step we shall make use of the proper 22-coloring problem (see Examples 1.2 and 1.4), which is typically hard to solve “globally,” but admits well-behaved “local” solutions.

To begin with, we convert a toast into a labeling using the following definition:

Definition 3.1 (From ℛ\mathcal{R} to fℛf_{\mathcal{R}}).

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free action. We define the outer boundary of a set A⊆XA\subseteq X to be ∂+A≔∂(X∖A)\partial^{+}A\coloneqq\partial(X\setminus A), i.e., x∈∂+Ax\in\partial^{+}A if and only if x∉Ax\notin A and 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,A)=1\mathsf{dist}(x,A)=1. Given a qq-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} for q⩾1q\geqslant 1, we let ∂+ℛ≔⋃K∈ℛ∂+K\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}\coloneqq\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal{R}}\partial^{+}K and define a map fℛ:X→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}f_{\mathcal{R}}\colon X\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\} by

fℛ​(x)≔{𝚁if ​x∈∂ℛ,𝙱if ​x∈∂+ℛ,𝙶otherwise.f_{\mathcal{R}}(x)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\mathtt{R}&\text{if }x\in\partial\mathcal{R},\\ \mathtt{B}&\text{if }x\in\partial^{+}\mathcal{R},\\ \mathtt{G}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

To phrase Definition 3.1 another way, we color the points on the boundary of each piece Red, the points adjacent to some piece from the outside Blue, and the other points Green. This construction is illustrated in Fig. 4. Note that, since q⩾1q\geqslant 1, ∂ℛ∩∂+ℛ=∅\partial\mathcal{R}\cap\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}=\varnothing, so fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} is well-defined.

Roughly, the solutions to our LCL problem 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q) will be the {𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\}-colorings that “locally” look as if they came from this construction:

Definition 3.2.

Given q⩾4q\geqslant 4, we define the LCL problem 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)≔([0,2​q]n,{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶},𝒜)\mathsf{RT}(q)\coloneqq([0,2q]^{n},\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\},\mathcal{A}), where

𝒜≔{φ:[0,2q]n→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}:φ=fℛ|[0,2​q]n for some rectangular q-toast ℛ⊆[ℤn]<∞}.\mathcal{A}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\varphi\colon[0,2q]^{n}\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\}\;:\;\varphi={{f_{\mathcal{R}}}|_{[0,2q]^{n}}}\text{ for some rectangular $q$-toast $\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}}]^{{<\infty}}}$}\big\}.

Here and in the sequel, we view ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} as acting on itself by translation. Note that in Definition 3.2, as well as in the rest of this section, we for convenience assume q⩾4q\geqslant 4.

If ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free action, then a function f:X→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}f\colon X\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\} is an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling of XX if and only if for every 2​q2q-square QQ in XX, there exists a rectangular qq-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}} such that ff agrees with fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} on QQ. In particular, for any rectangular qq-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}, the map fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} is an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling by definition. We wish to establish a converse to this fact: given an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling ff, we would like to find a rectangular qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R} with f=fℛf=f_{\mathcal{R}}. Unfortunately, this is not always possible. For instance, consider the map f:ℤ2→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}f\colon\mathbb{Z}^{2}\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\} given by

f⁡(x,y)≔{𝚁if ​x=0,𝙱if ​x=1,𝙶otherwise.f(x,y)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\mathtt{R}&\text{if }x=0,\\ \mathtt{B}&\text{if }x=1,\\ \mathtt{G}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

This is an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}. Indeed, the labeling around each point of the form (0,y)(0,y) locally looks as if that point is on the right boundary of a very large rectangle. However, this labeling clearly does not come from a rectangular toast. Notice, though, that ff would come from a rectangular toast if we allowed the “infinite rectangle” (−∞,0]×(−∞,∞)(-\infty,0]\times(-\infty,\infty) to be included. It turns out that, modulo allowing such “infinite rectangles,” 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labelings really do correspond to rectangular qq-toasts.

Before stating this result precisely, we need some extra notation. Let 𝖾1\mathsf{e}_{1}, …, 𝖾n\mathsf{e}_{n} be the standard generators of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Given a free action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, we let G⁡(X)G(X) be the graph with V⁡(G⁡(X))≔XV(G(X))\coloneqq X and

E(G(X))≔{{x,y}∈[X]2:𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍(x,y)=1}={{x,𝖾i⋅x}:x∈X, 1⩽i⩽n}.E(G(X))\,\coloneqq\,\{\{x,y\}\in[X]^{2}\,:\,\mathsf{dist}(x,y)=1\}\,=\,\{\{x,\mathsf{e}_{i}\cdot x\}\,:\,x\in X,\,1\leqslant i\leqslant n\}.

Note that 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍\mathsf{dist} is precisely the path metric on G⁡(X)G(X). In the special case when X=ℤnX=\mathbb{Z}^{n} and ℤn⮌ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathbb{Z}^{n} is the translation action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} on itself, we let Gn≔G⁡(ℤn)G_{n}\coloneqq G(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and observe that GnG_{n} is the Cayley graph 𝖢𝖺𝗒⁡(ℤn,{𝖾1,…,𝖾n})\mathsf{Cay}(\mathbb{Z}^{n},\{\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{e}_{n}\}). Note that for every free action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, every connected component of G⁡(X)G(X) is isomorphic to GnG_{n}. For any graph GG and a set U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G), we let G⁡[U]G[U] be the subgraph of GG induced by UU, i.e., the graph with vertex set UU and edge set E⁡(G)∩[U]2E(G)\cap[U]^{2}. An interval in ℤ\mathbb{Z} is a set of the form [a,b][a,b], [a,+∞)≔{c∈ℤ:a⩽c}[a,+\infty)\coloneqq\{c\in\mathbb{Z}\,:\,a\leqslant c\}, (−∞,b)≔{c∈ℤ:c⩽b}(-\infty,b)\coloneqq\{c\in\mathbb{Z}\,:\,c\leqslant b\}, or (−∞,+∞)≔ℤ(-\infty,+\infty)\coloneqq\mathbb{Z}, where a⩽ba\leqslant b are integers.

Lemma 3.3.

Let f:ℤn→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}f\colon\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\} be an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Consider an arbitrary connected component CC of the induced subgraph Gn​[f−1​(𝚁)]G_{n}[f^{-1}(\mathtt{R})]. Let R≔V⁡(C)R\coloneqq V(C) and let BB be the set of all points in f−1​(𝙱)f^{-1}(\mathtt{B}) having a neighbor in RR. Then R=∂SR=\partial S and B=∂+SB=\partial^{+}S for some set SS of the form S=I1×⋯×InS=I_{1}\times\cdots\times I_{n}, where I1I_{1}, …, InI_{n} are (possibly infinite) intervals in ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

Let E⊆E⁡(Gn)E\subseteq E(G_{n}) be the set of all edges with one endpoint in BB and the other one in RR; we call such edges bad. Let HH be the subgraph of GnG_{n} obtained by deleting the bad edges; that is, V⁡(H)≔ℤnV(H)\coloneqq\mathbb{Z}^{n} and E⁡(H)≔E⁡(Gn)∖EE(H)\coloneqq E(G_{n})\setminus E.

The following claim is the key to our argument:

Claim 3.4 (RR and BB are separated in HH).

The set RR is contained in a single component of the graph HH, and that component is disjoint from BB (hence HH has at least two components).

With a little more work, one can show that HH has exactly two components, one containing RR and the other one BB; we will not need this, however.

Intuitively, Claim 3.4 can be thought of as a discretized version of the Jordan–Brouwer separation theorem from topology, which says that a connected closed topological (n−1)(n-1)-manifold embedded in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} separates ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} into exactly two connected sets. This intuition informs our proof of the claim, which uses a discretized version of the mod 2 intersection theory that appears in some proofs of the Jordan–Brouwer theorem.

Proof of Claim 3.4.

It suffices to prove the following subclaim: Every cycle in GnG_{n} contains an even number of bad edges. This implies the claim as follows. First, it is clear that RR is contained in a single component of HH since R=V⁡(C)R=V(C), CC is connected, and no edge in CC is bad. Hence, if the claim failed, there would be a path PP from RR to some y∈By\in B using no bad edges. By the definition of BB, there must be some x∈Rx\in R adjacent to yy in GnG_{n}. Since RR is in a single component of HH we may assume xx is the starting point of PP. Adding the edge {y,x}\{y,x\} to PP yields a cycle in GnG_{n} with a single bad edge (namely {y,x}\{y,x\}), contradicting the subclaim.

It is well known and easy to see that the binary cycle space of GnG_{n} is spanned by the 44-cycles. (For example, this follows from the fact that the relations 𝖾i+𝖾j=𝖾j+𝖾i\mathsf{e}_{i}+\mathsf{e}_{j}=\mathsf{e}_{j}+\mathsf{e}_{i} for 1⩽i<j⩽n1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n give a presentation of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}.) Thus it suffices to verify the subclaim for 4-cycles.

So, let Σ\Sigma be a 4-cycle in GnG_{n}. If none of its vertices are in RR, then Σ\Sigma contains no bad edges. Now suppose that V⁡(Σ)∩R≠∅V(\Sigma)\cap R\neq\varnothing and take an arbitrary vertex w∈V⁡(Σ)∩Rw\in V(\Sigma)\cap R. Since ff is an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling, there exists a rectangular qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R} such that ff and fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} agree on V⁡(Σ)V(\Sigma). Since f⁡(w)=𝚁f(w)=\mathtt{R}, there is a rectangle K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} such that w∈∂Kw\in\partial K. Moreover, as q⩾4q\geqslant 4, Σ\Sigma cannot meet any other rectangle in ℛ\mathcal{R}. Thus, an edge of Σ\Sigma is bad if and only if it has one endpoint in KK and the other one not in KK. Since the cycle starts and ends at w∈Kw\in K, the number of such edges must be even. ∎

Let SS be the vertex set of the component of HH that contains RR. We claim that ∂S=R\partial S=R. Indeed, any x∈∂Sx\in\partial S must be an endpoint of a bad edge, and since x∉Bx\notin B by Claim 3.4, it follows that x∈Rx\in R. For the other direction, if x∈Rx\in R, then, by the definition of 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q), there is a point y∈By\in B adjacent to xx. By Claim 3.4, y∉Sy\notin S, so x∈∂Sx\in\partial S, as desired. A similar argument shows that ∂+S=B\partial^{+}S=B.

It remains to show that SS is a product of intervals. We will establish this by showing that SS is “locally convex” in the following sense:

Claim 3.5.

Let (w,x,y,z)(w,x,y,z) be a 4-cycle in GnG_{n} with ww, xx, y∈Sy\in S. Then z∈Sz\in S.

Proof.

Since ∂S=R\partial S=R and ∂+S=B\partial^{+}S=B, if this fails we must have z∈Bz\in B while ww, y∈Ry\in R. However, we claim that if (w,x,y,z)(w,x,y,z) is a 4-cycle in GnG_{n} with f⁡(w)=f⁡(y)=𝚁f(w)=f(y)=\mathtt{R}, then f⁡(z)≠𝙱f(z)\neq\mathtt{B}. Indeed, let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a rectangular qq-toast such that ff and fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} agree on the vertices ww, xx, yy, zz and their neighbors. Then there are KK, K′∈ℛK^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} such that w∈∂Kw\in\partial K and y∈∂K′y\in\partial K^{\prime}. Since 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(w,y)=2\mathsf{dist}(w,y)=2 and q⩾4q\geqslant 4, we must have K=K′K=K^{\prime}. As ww, y∈Ky\in K and KK is a rectangle, it follows that z∈Kz\in K as well. For f⁡(z)f(z) to be 𝙱\mathtt{B}, then, there would need to be some other rectangle K′′≠KK^{\prime\prime}\neq K in ℛ\mathcal{R} with 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(z,K′′)=1\mathsf{dist}(z,K^{\prime\prime})=1. But then 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(y,∂K′′)=2\mathsf{dist}(y,\partial K^{\prime\prime})=2, which contradicts the definition of a qq-toast as y∈∂Ky\in\partial K. ∎

It remains to show that any GnG_{n}-connected set SS satisfying Claim 3.5 is a product of intervals. For any xx, y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z}, let I⁡(x,y)≔[min⁡(x,y),max⁡(x,y)]I(x,y)\coloneqq[\min(x,y),\max(x,y)] be the interval between xx and yy, and for any x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), y=(y1,…,yn)∈ℤy=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}, let I(x,y)≔I(x1,y1)×⋯×I(xn,yn)I(x,y)\coloneqq I(x_{1},y_{1})\times\cdots\times I(x_{n},y_{n}). It suffices to show that for all xx, y∈Sy\in S, I⁡(x,y)⊆SI(x,y)\subseteq S.

We proceed by induction on the length of an x​yxy-path PP in Gn​[S]G_{n}[S]. In the base case x=yx=y, so I⁡(x,y)=I⁡(x,x)={x}I(x,y)=I(x,x)=\{x\} and there is nothing to show. For the inductive step, let zz be the penultimate vertex of PP. Then I⁡(x,z)⊆SI(x,z)\subseteq S by the inductive hypothesis. Without loss of generality, we may assume that y=𝖾1+zy=\mathsf{e}_{1}+z. Then

I(x,y)⊆I(x,z)∪({y1}×I(x2,y2)×⋯×I(xn,yn)).I(x,y)\,\subseteq\,I(x,z)\cup\big(\{y_{1}\}\times I(x_{2},y_{2})\times\cdots\times I(x_{n},y_{n})\big).

Calling the second set in this union TT, it remains to show that T⊆ST\subseteq S. To this end, take any w∈Tw\in T. Noting that TT is GnG_{n}-connected, we argue that w∈Sw\in S by induction on the length of a y​wyw-path QQ in Gn​[T]G_{n}[T]. In the base case w=y∈Sw=y\in S as desired. For the inductive step, let vv be the penultimate vertex of QQ. Then (v,w,w−𝖾1,v−𝖾1)(v,w,w-\mathsf{e}_{1},v-\mathsf{e}_{1}) is a 4-cycle in GnG_{n}. Since v∈Sv\in S by the inductive hypothesis and w−𝖾1w-\mathsf{e}_{1}, v−𝖾1v-\mathsf{e}_{1} are in I⁡(x,z)⊆SI(x,z)\subseteq S, we have w∈Sw\in S by Claim 3.5, as desired. ∎

We can now state the main result of this section: if an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} does not come from a rectangular qq-toast, then it must contain infinite rays of red, blue, and green points.

Lemma 3.6.

Let f:ℤn→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}f\colon\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\} be an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Exactly one of the following holds:

  1. (RT1)

    f=fℛf=f_{\mathcal{R}} for a rectangular qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R}, or

  2. (RT2)

    there exist x∈ℤnx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} and orthogonal 𝖽\mathsf{d}, 𝖽′∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}^{\prime}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\} such that for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N},

    f(i𝖽+x)=𝚁,f(i𝖽+𝖽′+x)=𝙱,andf(i𝖽+2𝖽′+x)=𝙶.f(i\mathsf{d}+x)\,=\,\mathtt{R},\quad f(i\mathsf{d}+\mathsf{d}^{\prime}+x)\,=\,\mathtt{B},\quad\text{and}\quad f(i\mathsf{d}+2\mathsf{d}^{\prime}+x)\,=\,\mathtt{G}.
Proof.

Options (RT1) and (RT2) are mutually exclusive since the rectangles in a rectangular qq-toast are finite. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the set of all components of the graph Gn​[f−1​(𝚁)]G_{n}[f^{-1}(\mathtt{R})]. For each C∈𝒞C\in\mathcal{C}, fix a set SCS_{C} such that ∂SC=V⁡(C)\partial S_{C}=V(C) and ∂+SC\partial^{+}S_{C} is the set of all blue points with a neighbor in V⁡(C)V(C), given by Lemma 3.3. Suppose for some C∈𝒞C\in\mathcal{C}, S≔SCS\coloneqq S_{C} is not a (finite) rectangle. Since SS is a product of intervals at least one of which is infinite and ∂S≠∅\partial S\neq\varnothing, we can choose x∈∂Sx\in\partial S and 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\} so that the set L≔{i​𝖽+x:i∈ℕ}L\coloneqq\{i\mathsf{d}+x\,:\,i\in\mathbb{N}\} is contained in ∂S⊆f−1​(𝚁)\partial S\subseteq f^{-1}(\mathtt{R}). Furthermore, there is some 𝖽′∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}^{\prime}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\} orthogonal to 𝖽\mathsf{d} such that L+𝖽′⊆∂+S⊆f−1​(𝙱)L+\mathsf{d}^{\prime}\subseteq\partial^{+}S\subseteq f^{-1}(\mathtt{B}). The definition of 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q) implies that for any y∈ℤny\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, if f⁡(y)=𝚁f(y)=\mathtt{R} and f⁡(𝖽′+y)=𝙱f(\mathsf{d}^{\prime}+y)=\mathtt{B}, then f⁡(2​𝖽′+y)=𝙶f(2\mathsf{d}^{\prime}+y)=\mathtt{G}. Hence, in this case (RT2) holds.

Now assume SCS_{C} is a finite rectangle for all C∈𝒞C\in\mathcal{C} and let ℛ≔{SC:C∈𝒞}\mathcal{R}\coloneqq\{S_{C}\,:\,C\in\mathcal{C}\}. Then ∂ℛ=f−1​(𝚁)\partial\mathcal{R}=f^{-1}(\mathtt{R}), and, since every blue vertex has a red neighbor, ∂+ℛ=f−1​(𝙱)\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}=f^{-1}(\mathtt{B}). Therefore, f=fℛf=f_{\mathcal{R}}. To confirm (RT1), it remains to verify that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a rectangular qq-toast.

Note first that all side lengths of each rectangle in ℛ\mathcal{R} are at least qq. Indeed, if, say, the ii-th side length of K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} is ℓ⩽q−1\ell\leqslant q-1, then there exists a point x∈∂+Kx\in\partial^{+}K such that

f⁡(x)=𝙱,f⁡(𝖾i+x)=f⁡(2​𝖾i+x)=⋯=f⁡((ℓ+1)​𝖾i+x)=𝚁,f⁡((ℓ+2)​𝖾i+x)=𝙱,f(x)\,=\,\mathtt{B},\quad f(\mathsf{e}_{i}+x)\,=\,f(2\mathsf{e}_{i}+x)\,=\,\cdots\,=\,f((\ell+1)\mathsf{e}_{i}+x)\,=\,\mathtt{R},\quad f((\ell+2)\mathsf{e}_{i}+x)\,=\,\mathtt{B},

which cannot occur in an 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling since ℓ+2⩽q+1<2​q\ell+2\leqslant q+1<2q.

Now suppose that there are K≠K′∈ℛK\neq K^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂K,∂K′)⩽q\mathsf{dist}(\partial K,\partial K^{\prime})\leqslant q. Let x∈∂Kx\in\partial K, x′∈∂K′x^{\prime}\in\partial K^{\prime} witness this. Then there is a square of side length qq, call it QQ, containing both xx and x′x^{\prime}. Using the definition of 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q), let ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} be a rectangular qq-toast such that ff agrees with fℛ′f_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime}} on QQ, and let LL, L′∈ℛ′L^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}^{\prime} be such that x∈∂Lx\in\partial L and x′∈∂L′x^{\prime}\in\partial L^{\prime}. Since 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,x′)⩽q\mathsf{dist}(x,x^{\prime})\leqslant q and ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} is a qq-toast, we must have L=L′L=L^{\prime}. Since every side length of LL is at least qq by the definition of a rectangular qq-toast, the graph Gn​[∂L∩Q]G_{n}[\partial L\cap Q] is connected. But x′∈∂L∩Q⊆f−1​(𝚁)x^{\prime}\in\partial L\cap Q\subseteq f^{-1}(\mathtt{R}), so x′x^{\prime} is in the same component of Gn​[f−1​(𝚁)]G_{n}[f^{-1}(\mathtt{R})] as xx, a contradiction. ∎

3.2.  Partial 2-colorings

At this point, we need to modify the problem 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q) in order to (a) avoid case (RT2) in Lemma 3.6, and (b) force the rectangular qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R} in case (RT1) to be complete. We will achieve these goals by requiring the green points to additionally carry a proper 22-coloring. (A similar idea appeared in the proof of [Bra+17, Thm. 6.1].) In this section we shall develop tools that will be employed to work with such 22-colorings later.

Remark 3.7.

It turns out that the ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-actions we shall work with automatically avoid case (RT2) away from a null/meager set, so the 22-coloring is only truly needed to guarantee completeness.

Definition 3.8 (Partial 22-colorings).

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free action. A partial 2-coloring of XX is a function c:X→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon X\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} such that if 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,y)=1\mathsf{dist}(x,y)=1 and c⁡(x)c(x), c⁡(y)∈{0,1}c(y)\in\{0,1\}, then c⁡(x)≠c⁡(y)c(x)\neq c(y). We say that a point x∈Xx\in X is uncolored if c⁡(x)=𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔c(x)=\mathtt{blank} and colored otherwise. The set of all colored points is denoted by 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)\mathsf{dom}(c).

Note that a partial 22-coloring is a solution to a certain LCL problem with labels {0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\}.

As we saw in Example 1.4, although the standard Cayley graph of ℤ\mathbb{Z} admits a proper 2-coloring, in the definable (e.g., Borel, measurable, etc.) context proper 2-colorings may fail to exist. The same is true for ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} with n⩾2n\geqslant 2, and, as we shall see, similar arguments impose restrictions on the domain of any Borel partial 2-coloring. Intuitively, Propositions 3.10 and 3.11 imply that under suitable assumptions on a ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, the domain of a Borel partial 22-coloring c:X→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon X\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} must “shatter” the graph G⁡(X)G(X) into several smaller components; for instance, it is not possible for 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)\mathsf{dom}(c) to have a connected intersection with every ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-orbit. We will also show in Proposition 3.12 that if a Borel set U⊆XU\subseteq X “shatters” XX into sufficiently small pieces—namely if G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] is component-finite—then we can find a Borel partial 22-coloring with domain UU.

Definition 3.9 (cc-Separated points).

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free action and let c:X→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon X\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} be a partial 22-coloring. We say that points xx, y∈Xy\in X are cc-separated if xx and yy belong to 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)\mathsf{dom}(c) and lie in different components of the graph G​(X)​[𝖽𝗈𝗆​(c)]G(X)[\mathsf{dom}(c)].

Recall that ℒ\mathcal{L} denotes the Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1], and ℒℤn\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}} the product measure.

Proposition 3.10.

Let c:ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} be a measurable partial 22-coloring such that ℒℤn​(𝖽𝗈𝗆​(c))>0\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(\mathsf{dom}(c))>0. Then for every 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\}, there exist x∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)x\in\mathsf{dom}(c) and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that the points xx and k​𝖽⋅xk\mathsf{d}\cdot x are cc-separated.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, c−1​(0)c^{-1}(0) has positive measure. By the regularity of measure [Kec95, Thm. 17.10], there exist a finite set S⊂ℤnS\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n} and nonempty open sets Us⊆[0,1]U_{s}\subseteq[0,1] for each s∈Ss\in S such that, if x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is chosen at random according to ℒℤn\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}, then

ℙ⁡[c⁡(x)=0∣x⁡(s)∈Us​ for all ​s∈S]⩾23.\mathbb{P}\big[c(x)=0\,\mid\,x(s)\in U_{s}\text{ for all }s\in S\big]\,\geqslant\,\frac{2}{3}.

Let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} be odd and large enough so that (k​𝖽+S)∩S=∅(k\mathsf{d}+S)\cap S=\varnothing. Now consider the nonempty open set WW of all x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) such that for each s∈Ss\in S, we have x⁡(s)x(s), x⁡(k​𝖽+s)∈Usx(k\mathsf{d}+s)\in U_{s}. By the union bound, the probability that c⁡(x)=c⁡(k​𝖽⋅x)=0c(x)=c(k\mathsf{d}\cdot x)=0 given x∈Wx\in W is at least 1/31/3. It follows that there exists some x∈Wx\in W with c⁡(x)=c⁡(k​𝖽⋅x)=0c(x)=c(k\mathsf{d}\cdot x)=0. We claim that this point xx is as desired.

If not, the graph G⁡(ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn))G(\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})) has a path PP from xx to k​𝖽⋅xk\mathsf{d}\cdot x contained in 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)\mathsf{dom}(c). Note that every component of G⁡(ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn))G(\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})) is isomorphic to the bipartite graph GnG_{n}. Thus, since kk is odd, every path in G⁡(ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn))G(\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})) from xx to k​d⋅xkd\cdot x, including PP, has an odd length. But this is impossible since c⁡(x)=c⁡(k​𝖽⋅x)=0c(x)=c(k\mathsf{d}\cdot x)=0 and the colors 00 and 11 must alternate between 00 and 11 along PP. ∎

Proposition 3.11.

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free continuous action on a Polish space XX. Suppose that for some 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\}, there is y∈Xy\in X such that the set {2​i​𝖽⋅y:i∈ℕ}\{2i\mathsf{d}\cdot y\,:\,i\in\mathbb{N}\} is dense. Then, if c:X→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon X\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} is a Baire-measurable partial 22-coloring and 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)\mathsf{dom}(c) is nonmeager, then there are x∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)x\in\mathsf{dom}(c) and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that the points xx and k​𝖽⋅xk\mathsf{d}\cdot x are cc-separated.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, c−1​(0)c^{-1}(0) is nonmeager. By [Tse22, Prop. 9.8], there is a nonempty open set U⊆XU\subseteq X such that c⁡(x)=0c(x)=0 for a comeager set of points x∈Ux\in U. Let U′≔⋃i∈ℤ((2​i+1)​𝖽⋅U)U^{\prime}\coloneqq\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}((2i+1)\mathsf{d}\cdot U) (note that here the union is over all i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, not just i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}). By construction, if x∈U′x\in U^{\prime}, then 2​i​𝖽⋅x∈U′2i\mathsf{d}\cdot x\in U^{\prime} for all i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}. Since U′U^{\prime} is open and {2​i​𝖽⋅y:i∈ℕ}\{2i\mathsf{d}\cdot y\,:\,i\in\mathbb{N}\} is dense, there is i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N} such that 2​i​𝖽⋅y∈U′2i\mathsf{d}\cdot y\in U^{\prime}. This implies that in fact 2​i​𝖽⋅y∈U′2i\mathsf{d}\cdot y\in U^{\prime} for all i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, so U′U^{\prime} is dense. It follows that U∩U′≠∅U\cap U^{\prime}\neq\varnothing, i.e., U∩((2​i+1)​𝖽⋅U)≠∅U\cap((2i+1)\mathsf{d}\cdot U)\neq\varnothing for some i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

For a comeager set of points x∈U∩((2​i+1)​𝖽⋅U)x\in U\cap((2i+1)\mathsf{d}\cdot U), we have c(x)=c(−(2i+1)𝖽⋅x)=0c(x)=c(-(2i+1)\mathsf{d}\cdot x)=0. Fix any such xx and let k≔2​i+1k\coloneqq 2i+1 (if k<0k<0, swap the roles of xx and k​𝖽⋅xk\mathsf{d}\cdot x). The rest of the argument is the same as in the proof of Proposition 3.10. ∎

On the other hand, we have the following positive results:

Proposition 3.12.

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free Borel action on a standard Borel space and let U⊆XU\subseteq X be a Borel set such that the graph G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] is component-finite. Then XX admits a Borel partial 22-coloring cc with 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(c)=U\mathsf{dom}(c)=U.

Proof.

This is a standard fact in descriptive combinatorics and an instance of the general principle that Borel combinatorics trivializes on component-finite graphs. In a sentence, we can find a Borel set meeting each component of G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] exactly once and define c⁡(x)c(x) for x∈Ux\in U to be the distance mod 22 from xx to the chosen point in its component. See [BW23, Pik21]for details. ∎

Proposition 3.13.

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free computable action on a computable set X⊆ℕX\subseteq\mathbb{N} and let U⊆XU\subseteq X be a computable subset such that the graph G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] is component-finite. Then XX admits a computable partial 22-coloring cc with domain UU.

Proof.

We apply the same idea as in the proof of Proposition 3.12. The function h:U→[U]<∞h\colon U\to{[{{U}}]^{{<\infty}}} sending a point to the vertex set of its component in G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] is clearly computable. Now, given x∈Ux\in U, we let c⁡(x)c(x) be the distance mod 22 from xx to, say, min⁡h⁡(x)\min h(x). ∎

3.3.  The colored rectangular qq-toast problem

We are now ready to define the LCL problem Π\Pi that witnesses Theorem 1.24.

Definition 3.14.

Let π:{𝚁,𝙱,0,1}→{𝚁,𝙱,𝙶}\pi\colon\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},0,1\}\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},\mathtt{G}\} and τ:{𝚁,𝙱,0,1}→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}\tau\colon\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},0,1\}\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} be given by

π⁡(𝚁)≔𝚁,π⁡(𝙱)≔𝙱,π⁡(0)≔𝙶,π⁡(1)≔𝙶,τ⁡(𝚁)≔𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔,τ⁡(𝙱)≔𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔,τ⁡(0)≔ 0,τ⁡(1)≔ 1.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{llll}\pi(\mathtt{R})\,\coloneqq\,\mathtt{R},&\pi(\mathtt{B})\,\coloneqq\,\mathtt{B},&\pi(0)\,\coloneqq\,\mathtt{G},&\pi(1)\,\coloneqq\,\mathtt{G},\\ \tau(\mathtt{R})\,\coloneqq\,\mathtt{blank},&\tau(\mathtt{B})\,\coloneqq\,\mathtt{blank},&\tau(0)\,\coloneqq\,0,&\tau(1)\,\coloneqq\,1.\end{array}

Given q⩾4q\geqslant 4, we let 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q) be the LCL problem with labels {𝚁,𝙱,0,1}\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},0,1\} whose solutions are precisely the functions ff such that:

  1. (C1)

    π∘f\pi\circ f is a solution to 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q), and

  2. (C2)

    τ∘f\tau\circ f is a partial 2-coloring.

In other words, to solve 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q), we must first find a solution to 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q) and then a partial 2-coloring whose domain is the set of green points. This is clearly an LCL problem with window [0,2​q]n[0,2q]^{n}. Our claim now is that taking Π=𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\Pi=\mathsf{CRT}(q) for any q⩾4q\geqslant 4 fulfils all the requirements of Theorem 1.24.

We start with the positive parts of Theorem 1.24. Parts (i) and (iii) follow from the following lemma together with Propositions 2.6 and 2.13 respectively:

Lemma 3.15.

If q⩾4q\geqslant 4 and ℛ\mathcal{R} is a Borel rectangular qq-toast for some free Borel action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X on a standard Borel space XX, then XX admits a 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling ff such that π∘f=fℛ\pi\circ f=f_{\mathcal{R}} and whose restriction to the set ⋃ℛ\bigcup{\mathcal{R}} is Borel.

Proof.

Note that fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} is a Borel 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling of XX. Let U≔fℛ−1​(𝙶)∩⋃ℛU\coloneqq f_{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}(\mathtt{G})\cap\bigcup\mathcal{R}. Observe that the graph G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] is component-finite. Indeed, if x∈Ux\in U, then fℛ​(x)=𝙶f_{\mathcal{R}}(x)=\mathtt{G} and there is a rectangle K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} such that x∈Kx\in K. This implies that the component of G​(X)​[U]G(X)[U] containing xx is included in K∖∂KK\setminus\partial K, which is a finite set, as desired. Hence, by Proposition 3.12, there exists a Borel partial 22-coloring c:X→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon X\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} with domain UU. On the other hand, the graph G⁡(X)G(X) is bipartite, so there exists a (possibly non-Borel) proper 22-coloring c′:X→{0,1}c^{\prime}\colon X\to\{0,1\} of G⁡(X)G(X) (i.e., a partial 22-coloring with domain XX). It remains to set

f⁡(x)≔{fℛ​(x)if ​fℛ​(x)∈{𝚁,𝙱},c⁡(x)if ​x∈U,c′​(x)otherwise.∎f(x)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}f_{\mathcal{R}}(x)&\text{if }f_{\mathcal{R}}(x)\in\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B}\},\\ c(x)&\text{if }x\in U,\\ c^{\prime}(x)&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\qed

Theorem 1.24(i) now follows by invoking Proposition 2.6 and Lemma 3.15 to obtain a 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling that is Borel on a conull set (namely on ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} for the square qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R} provided by Proposition 2.6), and hence measurable. Theorem 1.24(iii) follows in exactly the same way from Proposition 2.13 and Lemma 3.15. To prove Theorem 1.24(v), we apply the following version of Lemma 3.15 in the computable setting:

Lemma 3.16.

If q⩾4q\geqslant 4 and ℛ\mathcal{R} is a computable complete rectangular qq-toast for a free computable action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, then XX admits a computable 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling ff such that π∘f=fℛ\pi\circ f=f_{\mathcal{R}}.

Proof.

The construction is the same as the proof of Lemma 3.15 but with Proposition 3.13 used in place of Proposition 3.12. (Note that since ℛ\mathcal{R} is complete, the “otherwise” case in the definition of ff does not occur.) ∎

Theorem 1.24(v) is an immediate consequence of Proposition 2.18 and Lemma 3.16.

Now we turn our attention to the negative parts of Theorem 1.24, i.e., to items (ii) and (iv). Before we proceed, we require one more combinatorial fact about rectangular toasts, stated in the next lemma. It is related to the Hex Theorem [Gal79]; we give a direct proof here.

Lemma 3.17.

Let ℛ⊆[ℤn]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}}]^{{<\infty}}} be a rectangular qq-toast, where q⩾4q\geqslant 4. In the labeling fℛf_{\mathcal{R}}, any two green points in ℤn∖⋃ℛ\mathbb{Z}^{n}\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R} are joined by a path in the graph GnG_{n} all of whose vertices are green.

Proof.

It is clear from the definition of fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} that fℛ−1​(𝙶)∖⋃ℛf_{\mathcal{R}}^{-1}(\mathtt{G})\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R} is exactly the set of points whose distance from ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is at least 2. Let xx and yy be two such points and let P=(x=x0,x1,…,xℓ=y)P=(x=x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{\ell}=y) be an x​yxy-path in GnG_{n} minimizing |V⁡(P)∩∂+ℛ||V(P)\cap\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}|. If V⁡(P)∩∂+ℛ=∅V(P)\cap\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}=\varnothing, then PP stays at distance at least 22 from ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R}, so every vertex of PP is green, as desired. Otherwise, let K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} be a rectangle such that V⁡(P)∩∂+K≠∅V(P)\cap\partial^{+}K\neq\varnothing and let ss, tt be the minimum and maximum indices such that xsx_{s}, xt∈∂+Kx_{t}\in\partial^{+}K, respectively. Since xx has distance at least 2 from KK, we must have s>0s>0 and, by the choice of ss, 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(xs−1,K)=2\mathsf{dist}(x_{s-1},K)=2. Similarly, t<nt<n and 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(xt+1,K)=2\mathsf{dist}(x_{t+1},K)=2. We can then replace the segment of PP between xs−1x_{s-1} and xt+1x_{t+1} by an xs−1​xt+1x_{s-1}x_{t+1}-path QQ that stays at distance 22 or 33 from KK, resulting in a new x​yxy-path P′P^{\prime}. Since q⩾4q\geqslant 4, V⁡(Q)∩∂+ℛ=∅V(Q)\cap\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}=\varnothing, so we have |V⁡(P′)∩∂+ℛ|<|V⁡(P)∩∂+ℛ||V(P^{\prime})\cap\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}|<|V(P)\cap\partial^{+}\mathcal{R}|, contradicting the choice of PP. ∎

With Lemma 3.17 in hand, we can now prove Theorem 1.24(iv):

Proposition 3.18.

If q⩾4q\geqslant 4, then here is no finitary 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling f:ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)→{𝚁,𝙱,0,1}f\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},0,1\}.

Proof.

Before proceeding, we note that Lemmas 3.6 and 3.17, although stated for qq-toasts on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}, can be applied to any free transitive action of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}, since such an action is isomorphic to the translation action ℤn⮌ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathbb{Z}^{n}. To put this another way, given a free action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X and a rectangular qq-toast ℛ⊆[X]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}, we may apply Lemmas 3.6 and 3.17 separately on every ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-orbit 𝒪⊆X\mathcal{O}\subseteq X.

Suppose ff is a finitary 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling of ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}). For 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\}, let U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}} be the set of all points x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) such that f⁡(i​𝖽⋅x)=𝙶f(i\mathsf{d}\cdot x)=\mathtt{G} for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. Since ff is a measurable function, U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}} is a measurable set.

Claim 3.19.

The set U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}} is null for every 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\}.

Proof.

Note that the map c:ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)→{0,1,𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔}c\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})\to\{0,1,\mathtt{blank}\} that agrees with ff on U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}} and sends each x∉U𝖽x\notin U_{\mathsf{d}} to 𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔\mathtt{blank} is a partial 22-coloring with domain U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}}. Thus, if U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}} has positive measure, then by Proposition 3.10, there exist x∈U𝖽x\in U_{\mathsf{d}} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that xx and k​𝖽⋅xk\mathsf{d}\cdot x are cc-separated. But that is impossible as (x,𝖽⋅x,…,k​𝖽⋅x)(x,\mathsf{d}\cdot x,\ldots,k\mathsf{d}\cdot x) is a path from xx to k​𝖽⋅xk\mathsf{d}\cdot x contained in U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}}. ∎

Let N⊆ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)N\subseteq\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) be a null Borel set such that ff is Borel on the complement of NN (which exists since ff is measurable). Let M⊆ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)M\subseteq\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}) be a null Borel set containing ⋃𝖽U𝖽\bigcup_{\mathsf{d}}U_{\mathsf{d}}, where the union is over all 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\} (such a set MM which exists by Claim 3.19). Consider the following ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-invariant Borel subset X⊆ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)X\subseteq\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n}):

X≔ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤn)∖(ℤn⋅(N∪M))X\,\coloneqq\,\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{n})\setminus(\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cdot(N\cup M))

Since the shift action is measure-preserving, XX is conull. Let

ℛ≔{K∈[X]<∞:K is a rectangle such that f⁡(x)=𝚁 for all x∈∂K}.\mathcal{R}\,\coloneqq\,\{K\in{[{{X}}]^{{<\infty}}}\,:\,\text{$K$ is a rectangle such that $f(x)=\mathtt{R}$ for all $x\in\partial K$}\}.

The set ℛ\mathcal{R} is clearly Borel. Now we apply Lemma 3.6 to the 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling π∘f\pi\circ f on each orbit 𝒪\mathcal{O} of the shift action. Since, by construction, XX is disjoint from every U𝖽U_{\mathsf{d}}, case (RT1) must take place on all orbits 𝒪⊆X\mathcal{O}\subseteq X. This means that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a rectangular qq-toast and π∘f\pi\circ f agrees with fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} on XX.

Since XX is conull and ff is finitary, it follows that the characteristic function of ∂ℛ\partial\mathcal{R} is weakly finitary. By Proposition 2.16, this implies that ℒℤn​(⋃ℛ)<1\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(\bigcup\mathcal{R})<1. Since q⩾4q\geqslant 4, any point with distance 22 from some K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} is colored green by fℛf_{\mathcal{R}}. Therefore, the set

U≔{x∈X:fℛ​(x)=𝙶​ and ​x∉⋃ℛ}U\,\coloneqq\,\left\{x\in X\,:\,f_{\mathcal{R}}(x)=\mathtt{G}\text{ and }x\notin\bigcup\mathcal{R}\right\}

has positive measure, and the map cc that sends each x∈Ux\in U to f⁡(x)f(x) and all other points to 𝚋𝚕𝚊𝚗𝚔\mathtt{blank} is a Borel partial 22-coloring with domain UU. By Proposition 3.10, there exist x∈Ux\in U and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that xx and k​𝖾1⋅xk\mathsf{e}_{1}\cdot x are cc-separated. However, by Lemma 3.17 applied on the ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-orbit of xx, there is a path from xx to k​𝖾1⋅xk\mathsf{e}_{1}\cdot x contained in UU, which is a contradiction. ∎

Theorem 1.24(ii) is proved in a similar fashion:

Proposition 3.20.

Let ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X be a free continuous action on a nonempty compact Polish space XX such that for each 𝖽∈{±𝖾1,…,±𝖾n}\mathsf{d}\in\{\pm\mathsf{e}_{1},\ldots,\pm\mathsf{e}_{n}\}, the action of 2​𝖽2\mathsf{d} is minimal. Then XX does not admit a Baire-measurable 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling.

Proof.

The proof is exactly the same as the proof of Proposition 3.18, but with Propositions 3.11 and 2.12 taking the place of Propositions 3.10 and 2.16 respectively. (To apply Proposition 2.12, we observe that the minimality of the action of 2​𝖾12\mathsf{e}_{1} implies the same for 𝖾1\mathsf{e}_{1}.) ∎

The example following Proposition 2.12 (action on the circle via independent irrational rotations) again shows that an action as in Proposition 3.20 exists, proving item (ii) of Theorem 1.24.

4.  Adding extra structure: Proof of Theorem 1.25

In this section we prove Theorem 1.25. For simplicity, we only present the proof in the case n=2n=2; the general argument is the same, mutatis mutandis. In our construction we start with the problem 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q) used to witness Theorem 1.24 and then add some extra structure to it in order to ensure that the resulting problem can no longer be solved measurably on the free part of the shift, but still has a Baire-measurable solution on the free part of the shift as well as a computable solution on any free computable action. Similar (but much more complicated) arguments will be used in [Ber+] to prove Theorem 1.26.

Fix q⩾4q\geqslant 4 and let 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} be the LCL problem whose solutions on any free action ℤ2⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{2}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X are precisely the triples (f,h1,h2)(f,h_{1},h_{2}) with f:X→{𝚁,𝙱,0,1}f\colon X\to\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},0,1\} and h1h_{1}, h2:X→{0,1}h_{2}\colon X\to\{{{0}},{{1}}\} such that:

  1. (+1)

    ff is a solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q),

  2. (+2)

    if f⁡(x)=𝚁f(x)=\mathtt{R}, then h1​(x)=h2​(x)=0h_{1}(x)=h_{2}(x)={{0}},

  3. (+3)

    if f⁡(x)=𝙱f(x)=\mathtt{B} and f⁡(𝖾i⋅x)=𝚁f(\mathsf{e}_{i}\cdot x)=\mathtt{R}, then hi​(x)=1h_{i}(x)={{1}},

  4. (+4)

    if hi​(𝚎i⋅x)=hi​((𝚎1+𝚎2)⋅x)=1h_{i}(\mathtt{e}_{i}\cdot x)=h_{i}((\mathtt{e}_{1}+\mathtt{e}_{2})\cdot x)={1}, then hi​(x)=1h_{i}(x)={{1}}.

Clearly, 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} is an LCL problem on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with label set {𝚁,𝙱,0,1}×{0,1}2\{\mathtt{R},\mathtt{B},0,1\}\times\{{{0}},{{1}}\}^{2} and window [0,2​q]2[0,2q]^{2}. We claim that this problem has the properties stated in Theorem 1.25.

We start by considering what a solution (f,h1,h2)(f,h_{1},h_{2}) to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} (and hence also on an orbit of any free action of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}) must look like. Suppose we are in case (RT1) of Lemma 3.6 applied to the 𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{RT}(q)-labeling π∘f\pi\circ f and let ℛ⊆[ℤ2]<∞\mathcal{R}\subseteq{[{{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}}]^{{<\infty}}} be a rectangular qq-toast such that π∘f=fℛ\pi\circ f=f_{\mathcal{R}}. Take any rectangle K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R}. For concreteness, say K=[0,a]×[0,b]K=[0,a]\times[0,b]. Then for all t∈[0,b]t\in[0,b], we have f⁡(0,t)=𝚁f(0,t)=\mathtt{R} and f⁡(−1,t)=𝙱f(-1,t)=\mathtt{B}, so, by (+3), h1​(−1,t)=1h_{1}(-1,t)={1}. Applying (+4) iteratively, we then see that h1​(−1−i,t)=1h_{1}(-1-i,t)={1} for all 0⩽i⩽b0\leqslant i\leqslant b and 0⩽t⩽b−i0\leqslant t\leqslant b-i. Similarly, h2​(s,−1−i)=1h_{2}(s,-1-i)={1} for all 0⩽i⩽a0\leqslant i\leqslant a and 0⩽s⩽a−i0\leqslant s\leqslant a-i. This situation is illustrated in Fig. 5. Since, by (+2), ff cannot be equal to 𝚁\mathtt{R} when h1h_{1} or h2h_{2} is 1{1}, we conclude that the following must hold:

Claim 4.1.

Suppose (f,h1,h2)(f,h_{1},h_{2}) is a solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} on a free action ℤ2⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{2}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X, where π∘f=fℛ\pi\circ f=f_{\mathcal{R}} for a rectangular qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R}. Let K=([0,a]×[0,b])⋅x∈ℛK=([0,a]\times[0,b])\cdot x\in\mathcal{R} be a rectangle and let

D1​(K)\displaystyle D_{1}(K)\, ≔{(−1−i,t)⋅x: 0⩽i⩽b, 0⩽t⩽b−i},\displaystyle\coloneqq\,\{(-1-i,t)\cdot x\,:\,0\leqslant i\leqslant b,\,0\leqslant t\leqslant b-i\},
D2​(K)\displaystyle D_{2}(K)\, ≔{(s,−1−i)⋅x: 0⩽i⩽a, 0⩽s⩽a−i}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\,\{(s,-1-i)\cdot x\,:\,0\leqslant i\leqslant a,\,0\leqslant s\leqslant a-i\}.

Then (D1​(K)∪D2​(K))∩∂ℛ=∅(D_{1}(K)\cup D_{2}(K))\cap\partial\mathcal{R}=\varnothing.

It follows that in the setting of Claim 4.1, distinct rectangles KK, K′∈ℛK^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} satisfy D1​(K)∩D1​(K′)=∅D_{1}(K)\cap D_{1}(K^{\prime})=\varnothing and D2​(K)∩D2​(K′)=∅D_{2}(K)\cap D_{2}(K^{\prime})=\varnothing. Also, note that if KK is an (a×b)(a\times b)-rectangle, then

|D1​(K)|+|D2​(K)|\displaystyle|D_{1}(K)|+|D_{2}(K)|\, =(a+1)​(a+2)2+(b+1)​(b+2)2\displaystyle=\,\frac{(a+1)(a+2)}{2}+\frac{(b+1)(b+2)}{2}
(4.1) ⩾(a+1)2+(b+1)22⩾(a+1)​(b+1)=|K|.\displaystyle\geqslant\,\frac{(a+1)^{2}+(b+1)^{2}}{2}\,\geqslant\,(a+1)(b+1)\,=\,|K|.

We are now ready to show 𝖢𝖱𝖳+∉𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤ2)\mathsf{CRT}^{+}\notin\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{2}):

Claim 4.2.

There is no measurable solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} on ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤ2)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{2}) (i.e., 𝖢𝖱𝖳+∉𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤ2)\mathsf{CRT}^{+}\notin\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{2})).

Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that (f,h1,h2)(f,h_{1},h_{2}) is a measurable 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+}-labeling of ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤ2)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{2}). As in the proof of Proposition 3.18, we see that there is a Borel rectangular qq-toast ℛ\mathcal{R} such that π∘f\pi\circ f agrees with fℛf_{\mathcal{R}} almost everywhere. For a rectangle K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} with side lengths aa and bb, let its root be the point xx such that K=([0,a]×[0,b])⋅xK=([0,a]\times[0,b])\cdot x, and let RR be the set of all roots of the rectangles in ℛ\mathcal{R}. Also, for each x∈Rx\in R, let KxK_{x} be the unique rectangle in ℛ\mathcal{R} such that xx is its root. As discussed above, Claim 4.1 implies that for each i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, the sets {Di​(K):K∈ℛ}\{D_{i}(K)\,:\,K\in\mathcal{R}\} are pairwise disjoint. Since the action ℤ2⮌ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤ2)\mathbb{Z}^{2}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{2}) is measure-preserving, it follows that

∫x∈R|Di​(Kx)|​d​ℒℤ2​(x)=ℒℤ2​(⋃K∈ℛDi​(K))⩽ 1.\int_{x\in R}|D_{i}(K_{x})|\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}(x)\,=\,\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\left(\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal{R}}D_{i}(K)\right)\,\leqslant\,1.

Therefore, by (4.1),

∫x∈R|Kx|​d​ℒℤ2​(x)⩽∫x∈R(|D1​(Kx)|+|D2​(Kx)|)​d​ℒℤ2​(x)⩽ 2.\int_{x\in R}|K_{x}|\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}(x)\,\leqslant\,\int_{x\in R}\big(|D_{1}(K_{x})|+|D_{2}(K_{x})|\big)\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}(x)\,\leqslant\,2.

Using the invariance of the measure again, we see that the expected number of rectangles in ℛ\mathcal{R} containing a random point in ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤ2)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{2}) is at most 22. In particular, almost every point is contained in finitely many rectangles. By Lemma 2.5, this means that the set of all ℛ\mathcal{R}-complete points is null, i.e., ℒℤ2​(ℤ2⋅(X∖⋃ℛ))=1\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}(\mathbb{Z}^{2}\cdot(X\setminus\bigcup\mathcal{R}))=1, which implies that ℒℤ2​(⋃ℛ)<1\mathcal{L}^{\mathbb{Z}^{2}}(\bigcup\mathcal{R})<1. Now we use Proposition 3.10 and Lemma 3.17 to arrive at a contradiction in exactly the same way as in the last step of the proof of Proposition 3.18. ∎

Now we verify the other two properties of 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} stated in the theorem.

Claim 4.3.

There is a Baire-measurable solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} on ℱ⁡(2,ℤ2)\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) (i.e., 𝖢𝖱𝖳+∈𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(ℤ2)\mathsf{CRT}^{+}\in\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\mathbb{Z}^{2})).

Proof.

We modify the construction in the proof of Proposition 2.13. Define ρ:ℱ⁡(2,ℤ2)→2\rho\colon\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{2})\to 2 by ρ⁡(x)≔x⁡(𝟎)\rho(x)\coloneqq x(\bm{0}). Call a square KK in ℱ⁡(2,ℤ2)\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{2}) safe if

  • —

    the side length of KK, say NN, is at least qq,

  • —

    for all x∈Xx\in X:

    • —

      if x∈∂Kx\in\partial K, then ρ⁡(x)=1\rho(x)=1,

    • —

      if 0<𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,∂K)⩽q0<\mathsf{dist}(x,\partial K)\leqslant q, then ρ⁡(x)=0\rho(x)=0,

    • —

      and, additionally, if x∉Kx\notin K and 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(x,∂K)⩽2​N\mathsf{dist}(x,\partial K)\leqslant 2N, then ρ⁡(x)=0\rho(x)=0.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the set of all safe squares. The same argument as in the proof of Proposition 2.13 shows that ℛ\mathcal{R} is a square qq-toast and ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} is a comeager (in fact, dense open) set. (Note that the square RR used there to witness the density of ⋃ℛ\bigcup\mathcal{R} remains safe with the modified definition.) Then Lemma 3.15 yields a Baire-measurable 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling ff of ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤ2)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{2}) such that π∘f=fℛ\pi\circ f=f_{\mathcal{R}}. Note that if K∈ℛK\in\mathcal{R} is an NN-square, then for all K′∈ℛK^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} with K′⊈KK^{\prime}\not\subseteq K, we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂K,∂K′)>2​N\mathsf{dist}(\partial K,\partial K^{\prime})>2N. This implies that for each i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, the sets D1​(K)D_{1}(K) and D2​(K)D_{2}(K) are disjoint from ∂ℛ\partial\mathcal{R}. Therefore, letting

hi​(x)≔{1if ​x∈Di​(K)​ for some ​K∈ℛ,0otherwise,h_{i}(x)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}{1}&\text{if }x\in D_{i}(K)\text{ for some }K\in\mathcal{R},\\ {0}&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

we see that (f,h1,h2)(f,h_{1},h_{2}) is a Baire-measurable solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} on ℱ⁡([0,1],ℤ2)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\mathbb{Z}^{2}), as desired. ∎

Claim 4.4.

For every free computable action ℤ2⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{2}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X on a computable set X⊆ℕX\subseteq\mathbb{N}, there exists a computable solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} on XX. In other words, 𝖢𝖱𝖳+∈𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(ℤ2)\mathsf{CRT}^{+}\in\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{Z}^{2}).

Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that X=ℕX=\mathbb{N}. As in the proof of Proposition 2.18, we describe an algorithm that enumerates a sequence R0R_{0}, R1R_{1}, … with the following properties:

  • —

    each RiR_{i} is an NiN_{i}-square in XX for some Ni⩾i+qN_{i}\geqslant i+q,

  • —

    for all i≠ji\neq j, we have 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂Ri,∂Rj)>q\mathsf{dist}(\partial R_{i},\partial R_{j})>q,

  • —

    for all x∈ℕx\in\mathbb{N}, x∈Rxx\in R_{x},

  • —

    and, additionally, if Rj⊈RiR_{j}\not\subseteq R_{i}, then 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂Ri,∂Rj)>2​Ni\mathsf{dist}(\partial R_{i},\partial R_{j})>2N_{i}.

Namely, once R0R_{0}, …, Ri−1R_{i-1} have been computed, we cycle through the integers j⩾i+qj\geqslant i+q until we find one such for all t∈{0,…,i−1}t\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\},

𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂([−j,j]2⋅i),∂Rt)>max⁡{q,2​Nt},\mathsf{dist}(\partial([-j,j]^{2}\cdot i),\,\partial R_{t})\,>\,\max\{q,2N_{t}\},

and, moreover, if Rt⊈[−j,j]2R_{t}\not\subseteq[-j,j]^{2}, then

𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡(∂([−j,j]2⋅i),∂Rt)> 4​j.\mathsf{dist}(\partial([-j,j]^{2}\cdot i),\,\partial R_{t})\,>\,4j.

Such jj must exist since the set {R0,…,Ri−1}\{R_{0},\ldots,R_{i-1}\} is finite. We then let Ni≔2​jN_{i}\coloneqq 2j and Ri≔[−j,j]n⋅iR_{i}\coloneqq[-j,j]^{n}\cdot i.

As in the proof of Proposition 2.18, ℛ≔{Ri:i∈ℕ}\mathcal{R}\coloneqq\{R_{i}\,:\,i\in\mathbb{N}\} is a computable compete square qq-toast. Hence, by Lemma 3.16, there is a computable 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q)-labeling ff with π∘f=fℛ\pi\circ f=f_{\mathcal{R}}. As in the proof of Claim 4.3, we now set, for each i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\},

hi​(x)≔{1if ​x∈Di​(Rt)​ for some ​t∈ℕ,0otherwise.h_{i}(x)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}{1}&\text{if }x\in D_{i}(R_{t})\text{ for some }t\in\mathbb{N},\\ {0}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Notice that the function hih_{i} is computable, since if x∈Di​(Rt)x\in D_{i}(R_{t}) for some t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, then Rt⊆RxR_{t}\subseteq R_{x}, so t⩽Nxt\leqslant N_{x}. Thus, (f,h1,h2)(f,h_{1},h_{2}) is a computable solution to 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+}, as desired. ∎

We have now established all the required properties of 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+}, and thus the proof of Theorem 1.25 is complete.

5.  Proof of Theorem 1.19

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.19, i.e., that the inclusion 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)⊆𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(Γ)\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\Gamma) is valid for every group Γ\Gamma. As mentioned in the introduction, this result follows from the general analysis of the Baire-measurable combinatorics of the shift action presented in the paper [Ber21] by the second named author. The theory developed in [Ber21] is more general that what we require; below we only describe the tools necessary to deduce Theorem 1.19.

Fix a group Γ\Gamma and a finite set Λ\Lambda. Let 𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ)\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma) be the set of all partial maps φ:Γ⇢Λ\varphi\colon\Gamma\dashrightarrow\Lambda with finite domains. There is a natural shift action Γ⮌𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma) given by

(γ⋅φ)​(δ)≔φ⁡(δ​γ)for all γ, δ∈Γ and x∈𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ),(\gamma\cdot\varphi)(\delta)\,\coloneqq\,\varphi(\delta\gamma)\quad\text{for all $\gamma$, $\delta\in\Gamma$ and $x\in\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma)$},

where if δ​γ∉𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)\delta\gamma\notin\mathsf{dom}(\varphi), then (γ⋅φ)​(δ)(\gamma\cdot\varphi)(\delta) is left undefined. We also let γ⋅D≔D​γ−1\gamma\cdot D\coloneqq D\gamma^{-1} for every finite subset D⊆ΓD\subseteq\Gamma, so that 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(γ⋅φ)=γ⋅𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)\mathsf{dom}(\gamma\cdot\varphi)=\gamma\cdot\mathsf{dom}(\varphi). A (Λ,Γ)(\Lambda,\Gamma)-ideal is a set ℐ⊆𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ)\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma) that is invariant under the shift action of Γ\Gamma and closed under taking restrictions of functions. A (Λ,Γ)(\Lambda,\Gamma)-ideal ℐ\mathcal{I} is extendable if for all φ∈ℐ\varphi\in\mathcal{I} and γ∈Γ∖𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\mathsf{dom}(\varphi), there is some ψ∈ℐ\psi\in\mathcal{I} such that φ⊂ψ\varphi\subset\psi and γ∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ψ)\gamma\in\mathsf{dom}(\psi).

Definition 5.1 (Join property).

A (Λ,Γ)(\Lambda,\Gamma)-ideal ℐ\mathcal{I} has the join property if it is possible to assign to each φ∈ℐ\varphi\in\mathcal{I} a finite subset D⁡(φ)∈ΓD(\varphi)\in\Gamma so that, for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, φ1\varphi_{1}, …, φk∈ℐ\varphi_{k}\in\mathcal{I}, and γ1\gamma_{1}, …, γk∈Γ\gamma_{k}\in\Gamma, if the sets γ1⋅D⁡(φ1)\gamma_{1}\cdot D(\varphi_{1}), …, γk⋅D⁡(φk)\gamma_{k}\cdot D(\varphi_{k}) are pairwise disjoint, then (γ1⋅φ1)∪…∪(γk⋅φk)∈ℐ(\gamma_{1}\cdot\varphi_{1})\cup\ldots\cup(\gamma_{k}\cdot\varphi_{k})\in\mathcal{I}.

We can now state the (somewhat weakened form of the) result from [Ber21] that we shall use:

Theorem 5.2 (AB [Ber21, special case of Thm. 2.10]).

Let Γ\Gamma be a finitely generated group and let Π=(W,Λ,𝒜)\Pi=(W,\Lambda,\mathcal{A}) be an LCL problem on Γ\Gamma. Then Π∈𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(Γ)\Pi\in\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\Gamma) if and only if there exists an extendable (Λ,Γ)(\Lambda,\Gamma)-ideal ℐ⊆𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ)\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma) such that:

  • —

    each φ∈ℐ\varphi\in\mathcal{I} can be extended to a Π\Pi-labeling of Γ\Gamma, and

  • —

    ℐ\mathcal{I} has the join property.

With this, we are ready to prove Theorem 1.19.

Proof of Theorem 1.19.

The argument is similar to [Ber21, proof of Lem. 5.1], with measure taking the place of Baire category. Let Γ\Gamma be a finitely generated group and let Π=(W,Λ,𝒜)\Pi=(W,\Lambda,\mathcal{A}) be an LCL problem on Γ\Gamma. Suppose Π∈𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)\Pi\in\mathtt{FFIID}(\Gamma) and let f:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→Λf\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\Lambda be a finitary Π\Pi-labeling of ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma). We shall use ff to define a (Λ,Γ)(\Lambda,\Gamma)-ideal ℐ⊆𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ)\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma) satisfying the conditions of Theorem 5.2, from which it will follow that Π∈𝙱𝚊𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚂𝙷𝙸𝙵𝚃⁡(Γ)\Pi\in\mathtt{BaireSHIFT}(\Gamma), as desired.

Define a measurable Γ\Gamma-equivariant function π:ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)→𝒮⁡(Λ,Γ)\pi\colon\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\to\mathcal{S}(\Lambda,\Gamma) by

(π⁡(x))​(γ)≔f⁡(γ⋅x)for all x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ) and γ∈Γ.\big(\pi(x)\big)(\gamma)\,\coloneqq\,f(\gamma\cdot x)\quad\text{for all $x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)$ and $\gamma\in\Gamma$}.

Since ff is a solution to Π\Pi, π⁡(x)\pi(x) is a Π\Pi-labeling of Γ\Gamma for every x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma). For φ∈𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ)\varphi\in\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma), let Uφ⊆𝒮⁡(Λ,Γ)U_{\varphi}\subseteq\mathcal{S}(\Lambda,\Gamma) be the clopen set of all functions Γ→Λ\Gamma\to\Lambda that extend φ\varphi and define

ℐ≔{φ∈𝒮<∞​(Λ,Γ):π−1​(Uφ)​ has positive measure}.\mathcal{I}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{\varphi\in\mathcal{S}_{<\infty}(\Lambda,\Gamma)\,:\,\pi^{-1}(U_{\varphi})\text{ has positive measure}\big\}.

It is clear that, since the shift action Γ⮌ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) is measure-preserving, ℐ\mathcal{I} is a (Λ,Γ)(\Lambda,\Gamma)-ideal. Moreover, since π\pi sends points in ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma) to Π\Pi-labelings of Γ\Gamma, each member of ℐ\mathcal{I} can be extended to a Π\Pi-labeling of Γ\Gamma. It remains to verify that ℐ\mathcal{I} is extendable and has the join property.

Take any φ∈ℐ\varphi\in\mathcal{I} and γ∈Γ∖𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)\gamma\in\Gamma\setminus\mathsf{dom}(\varphi). For each λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, let φλ:𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)∪{γ}→Λ\varphi_{\lambda}\colon\mathsf{dom}(\varphi)\cup\{\gamma\}\to\Lambda be the mapping that agrees with φ\varphi on 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)\mathsf{dom}(\varphi) and sends γ\gamma to λ\lambda . Note that

Uφ=⋃λ∈ΛUφλ,henceπ−1​(Uφ)=⋃λ∈Λπ−1​(Uφλ).U_{\varphi}\,=\,\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}U_{\varphi_{\lambda}},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\pi^{-1}(U_{\varphi})\,=\,\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\pi^{-1}(U_{\varphi_{\lambda}}).

Since φ∈ℐ\varphi\in\mathcal{I}, the set π−1​(Uφ)\pi^{-1}(U_{\varphi}) has positive measure. It follows that for some λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, π−1​(Uφλ)\pi^{-1}(U_{\varphi_{\lambda}}) must also have positive measure, i.e., φλ∈ℐ\varphi_{\lambda}\in\mathcal{I}. This shows that ℐ\mathcal{I} is extendable.

Finally, we need to argue that ℐ\mathcal{I} has the join property. This is where we use that ff is finitary. Consider any φ∈ℐ\varphi\in\mathcal{I}. For each finite set D⊆ΓD\subseteq\Gamma, let

Xφ,D≔{x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ):π⁡(x′)∈Uφ for almost all x′∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ) that agree with x on D}.X_{\varphi,D}\,\coloneqq\,\big\{x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\,:\,\text{$\pi(x^{\prime})\in U_{\varphi}$ for almost all $x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)$ that agree with $x$ on $D$}\big\}.

Let us record the following observations, which follow immediately from the above definition:

  • —

    The set Xφ,DX_{\varphi,D} is measurable by Fubini’s theorem.

  • —

    The membership of a point xx in Xφ,DX_{\varphi,D} is determined by the restriction of xx to DD.

  • —

    For almost all x∈Xφ,Dx\in X_{\varphi,D}, we have π⁡(x)∈Uφ\pi(x)\in U_{\varphi}.

Since ff is finitary, almost every point x∈π−1​(Uφ)x\in\pi^{-1}(U_{\varphi}) belongs to Xφ,DX_{\varphi,D} for some finite set D⊆ΓD\subseteq\Gamma. Thus, we can pick a finite set D⁡(φ)⊆ΓD(\varphi)\subseteq\Gamma such that the measure of the set X⁡(φ)≔Xφ,D⁡(φ)X(\varphi)\coloneqq X_{\varphi,D(\varphi)} is positive.

Now take k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, φ1\varphi_{1}, …, φk∈ℐ\varphi_{k}\in\mathcal{I}, γ1\gamma_{1}, …, γk∈Γ\gamma_{k}\in\Gamma and suppose the sets γ1⋅D⁡(φ1)\gamma_{1}\cdot D(\varphi_{1}), …, γk⋅D⁡(φk)\gamma_{k}\cdot D(\varphi_{k}) are pairwise disjoint. Sample a random point x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ)x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma). Then, for each 1⩽i⩽k1\leqslant i\leqslant k, x∈γi⋅X⁡(φi)x\in\gamma_{i}\cdot X(\varphi_{i}) with positive probability. The random event Ei≔{x∈γi⋅X(φi)}E_{i}\coloneqq\{x\in\gamma_{i}\cdot X(\varphi_{i})\} is determined by the restriction of xx to γi⋅D⁡(φi)\gamma_{i}\cdot D(\varphi_{i}). Since the sets γ1⋅D⁡(φ1)\gamma_{1}\cdot D(\varphi_{1}), …, γk⋅D⁡(φk)\gamma_{k}\cdot D(\varphi_{k}) are disjoint, the events E1E_{1}, …, EkE_{k} are mutually independent, so with positive probability all of them occur simultaneously. In other words, the following set has positive measure:

E≔{x∈ℱ⁡([0,1],Γ):x∈γi⋅X⁡(φi)​ for all ​1⩽i⩽k}.E\,\coloneqq\,\{x\in\mathcal{F}([0,1],\Gamma)\,:\,x\in\gamma_{i}\cdot X(\varphi_{i})\text{ for all }1\leqslant i\leqslant k\}.

Note that for almost all x∈Ex\in E and for all 1⩽i⩽k1\leqslant i\leqslant k, we have π⁡(x)∈Uγi⋅φi\pi(x)\in U_{\gamma_{i}\cdot\varphi_{i}}, or, equivalently, π⁡(x)∈U(γ1⋅φ1)∪…∪(γk⋅φk)\pi(x)\in U_{(\gamma_{1}\cdot\varphi_{1})\cup\ldots\cup(\gamma_{k}\cdot\varphi_{k})}. Therefore, (γ1⋅φ1)∪…∪(γk⋅φk)∈ℐ(\gamma_{1}\cdot\varphi_{1})\cup\ldots\cup(\gamma_{k}\cdot\varphi_{k})\in\mathcal{I}, and the proof is complete. ∎

6.  Final remarks and open problems

6.1.  Unlabeled grids

Throughout this paper, we have been focusing on LCL problems that are defined on finitely generated groups (in particular, ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and their actions. In computer science and probability theory, it is also common to consider problems on “pure” graphs, without any additional structure. In the context of this paper, it is natural to ask whether our results extend to the framework of LCL problems on unlabeled, undirected nn-dimensional grids, i.e., graphs isomorphic to the standard Cayley graph GnG_{n} of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} (without edge directions or markers indicating which generator each edge corresponds to). The short answer is “yes,” with virtually the same proofs.

Formally, we can define an LCL problem on GnG_{n} as an LCL problem Π\Pi on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} such that the set of all Π\Pi-labelings of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is invariant under the natural action of the group 𝖠𝗎𝗍⁡(Gn)\mathsf{Aut}(G_{n}) of graph-theoretic automorphisms of GnG_{n}. Note that 𝖠𝗎𝗍⁡(Gn)\mathsf{Aut}(G_{n}) is generated by the group of translations of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} (which is isomorphic to ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and the group 𝖠𝗎𝗍∙​(Gn)\mathsf{Aut}_{\bullet}(G_{n}) of root-preserving automorphisms, i.e., the automorphisms φ:ℤn→ℤn\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to\mathbb{Z}^{n} satisfying φ⁡(𝟎)=𝟎\varphi(\bm{0})=\bm{0}. The group 𝖠𝗎𝗍∙​(Gn)\mathsf{Aut}_{\bullet}(G_{n}) is finite and generated by permutations and sign changes of the generators.

The role of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-actions in this setting is taken by GnG_{n}-graphs, i.e., graphs in which every connected component is isomorphic to GnG_{n}. If Π\Pi is an LCL problem on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and GG is a graph isomorphic to GnG_{n}, we call f:V⁡(G)→Λf\colon V(G)\to\Lambda a solution to Π\Pi on GG, or a Π\Pi-labeling of GG, if f∘φf\circ\varphi is a solution to Π\Pi on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} for any (hence every) isomorphism φ:ℤn→V⁡(G)\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to V(G). If GG is a GnG_{n}-graph, then f:V⁡(G)→Λf\colon V(G)\to\Lambda is a solution to Π\Pi on GG if it is a Π\Pi-labeling of each component of GG. Note that if ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X is a free action, then the corresponding graph G⁡(X)G(X) (as defined in §3.1 on p. 3.1) is a GnG_{n}-graph. Conversely, every GnG_{n}-graph is generated by a free ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-action in this way. However, not all Borel GnG_{n}-graphs are generated by free Borel ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-actions (even if n=1n=1 [KM04, Mil04]; see also [Tho21, §5] for an analysis of the n=2n=2 case). In other words, in this framework we consider a restricted class of LCL problems, but attempt to solve them on a broader class of structures.

The classes of LCL problems 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(Gn)\mathtt{BOREL}(G_{n}), 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Gn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(G_{n}), and so on are defined by modifying the definitions of 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), etc. in obvious ways. We now have the following analog of Theorem 1.24 in this setting:

To prove Theorem 6.1, we simply observe that the problem 𝖢𝖱𝖳⁡(q)\mathsf{CRT}(q) used to witness Theorem 1.24 is, in fact, an LCL problem on GnG_{n}, because the notions of a rectangular qq-toast and a partial 22-coloring are automorphism-invariant. This immediately shows that parts (ii), (iii), and (iv) of Theorem 6.1 follow from the corresponding items in Theorem 1.24. Modifying the arguments that go into proving parts (i) and (v) of Theorem 1.24 to make sure they apply to GnG_{n}-graphs and not just ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}-actions is routine, and we omit the details.

We conclude this discussion with two remarks. First, by taking the quotient under the natural action 𝖠𝗎𝗍∙​(Gn)⮌ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)\mathsf{Aut}_{\bullet}(G_{n})\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n}), it is not difficult to arrange the Baire-measurable labeling in item (iii) of Theorem 6.1 to be 𝖠𝗎𝗍∙​(Gn)\mathsf{Aut}_{\bullet}(G_{n})-invariant. Second, although the problem 𝖢𝖱𝖳+\mathsf{CRT}^{+} used in §4 to prove Theorem 1.25 is not an LCL problem on GnG_{n}, it is not hard to modify it to obtain an analogous version of Theorem 1.25 for unlabeled grids.

6.2.  Open problems

Many fundamental questions about the complexity of LCL problems on ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} remain open. Fig. 1 summarizes the current state of our knowledge of this matter, and any relation not shown there leads to an interesting open problem. Here we give a list of a few such problems that we find particularly intriguing. In what follows, nn is an integer at least 22.

Question 6.2.

Does the inclusion 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)⊂𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subset\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) hold? (If it does, it must be strict.)

Question 6.3.

Do we have 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)=𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})=\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})?

Question 6.4.

Do we have 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)=𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})=\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})?

Question 6.5.

What is the relationship between 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and 𝙱𝙾𝚁𝙴𝙻⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BOREL}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})? What about 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) and 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})? No inclusion between these classes has been ruled out yet.

Question 6.6.

Does the (necessarily strict) inclusion 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)⊂𝙲𝙾𝙼𝙿𝚄𝚃𝙰𝙱𝙻𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subset\mathtt{COMPUTABLE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) hold?

Question 6.7.

Call a free Borel action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X on a Polish space XX Baire-universal if 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is precisely the class of all LCL problems that admit a Baire-measurable solution on XX. Note that Baire-universal actions exist. Namely, for each LCL problem Π∉𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\Pi\notin\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}), we can fix a free Borel action ℤn⮌XΠ\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X_{\Pi} that has no Baire-measurable Π\Pi-labeling and then take the disjoint union of XΠX_{\Pi} over all Π∉𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\Pi\notin\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}). However, this is not a very satisfying example, since we do not know in general which problems are not in 𝙱𝙰𝙸𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤn)\mathtt{BAIRE}(\mathbb{Z}^{n}). Is there a more “natural,” “concrete” example of a Baire-universal action? The shift action ℤn⮌ℱ⁡(2,ℤn)\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}\mathcal{F}(2,\mathbb{Z}^{n}) is an obvious candidate, but it is not Baire-universal by Theorem 1.14. But what about, say, the action on the circle via independent irrational rotations (see the paragraph following Proposition 2.12)? Is it Baire-universal? More abstractly, does there exist a Baire-universal free continuous action ℤn⮌X\mathbb{Z}^{n}\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}X on a Polish space XX with a dense orbit (such actions are called generically ergodic [Tse22, Prop. 20.18])?

There are also plenty of interesting problems for other finitely generated groups. Even for free groups, which are by far the best understood, some questions remain unanswered. For example:

Question 6.8.

Do we have 𝙵𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(𝔽n)=𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{FFIID}(\mathbb{F}_{n})=\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{F}_{n}) or 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(𝔽n)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(𝔽n)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{F}_{n})=\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{F}_{n})? We conjecture the answer is “no” to both.

Furthermore, there remain general questions that are of interest for all finitely generated groups. Here are two examples, the first of which is closely related to Question 6.4.

Question 6.9.

Given a finitely generated group Γ\Gamma and a standard probability space (X,μ)(X,\mu), let 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(X,μ,Γ)\mathtt{FIID}(X,\mu,\Gamma) be the class of all LCL problems on Γ\Gamma that have a measurable solution on ℱ⁡(X,Γ)\mathcal{F}(X,\Gamma). As a special case, 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(Γ)=𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡([0,1],ℒ,Γ)\mathtt{FIID}(\Gamma)=\mathtt{FIID}([0,1],\mathcal{L},\Gamma), where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1]. Assuming μ\mu is not concentrated on a single point, does the class 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(X,μ,Γ)\mathtt{FIID}(X,\mu,\Gamma) depend on the space (X,μ)(X,\mu)? It does not when Γ=ℤ\Gamma=\mathbb{Z} (because 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤ)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤ)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z})=\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z})) and when Γ\Gamma is non-amenable by a result of Bowen [Bow19, Corl. 1.3]. But what about, say, Γ=ℤn\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{n}?

Question 6.10.

Let 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴𝗉𝗆𝗉​(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}_{\mathsf{pmp}}(\Gamma) be the class of all LCL problems on Γ\Gamma that admit a measurable solution on every free measure-preserving action Γ⮌(X,μ)\Gamma\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\righttoleftarrow$}}(X,\mu), where (X,μ)(X,\mu) is a standard probability space. Clearly, 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(Γ)⊆𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴𝗉𝗆𝗉​(Γ)\mathtt{MEASURE}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathtt{MEASURE}_{\mathsf{pmp}}(\Gamma). Can this inclusion be strict? Once again, we know 𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴𝗉𝗆𝗉​(ℤ)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴​(ℤ)\mathtt{MEASURE}_{\mathsf{pmp}}(\mathbb{Z})=\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}) because 𝙵𝙸𝙸𝙳⁡(ℤ)=𝙼𝙴𝙰𝚂𝚄𝚁𝙴⁡(ℤ)\mathtt{FIID}(\mathbb{Z})=\mathtt{MEASURE}(\mathbb{Z}), but we do not know the answer for any group that is not virtually ℤ\mathbb{Z}.
